This technique utilizes optimized single-photon detection, enabling measurement of entanglement of arbitrarily large two-qubit systems, including those encoded in spatial modes, polarization, or orbital angular momentum.
We demonstrate applications in measuring entanglement of two photons and potential use in quantum information processing.

The reduction of anomalous transport in the minor radius shear region of a reverse-shear H-mode plasma in the JET tokamak can be attributed to the formation of palm tree structures formed by a combination of ITG and TAE modes, which are connected by the ITG mode driven turbulence and the non-local free energy source. The formation of these palm tree structures is a result of the interaction between the modes and the radial flow field, which causes the modes to align and propagate along the same path. The phases of the modes are also found to be correlated, which indicates a strong coupling between the modes. The presence of these palm tree structures is believed to be responsible for the formation of the pedestal and the impurity profiles observed in the plasma.

This study evaluates the performance of a simple, no-cost baseline, in which the base model, architecture, and hyperparameters are fixed and manually chosen, and the only variable is the set of pre-trained models being tested. A straightforward baseline that mirrors human practice of using a single, suitably pre-trained model provides a strong anchor for the learning process in continuous learning. When compared to this baseline, many of the recently proposed pre-trained models, when used in the context of continuous learning, actually perform worse than expected and offer little advantage over a simple, basic approach. A pre-trained model is not necessarily a guarantee of superior continuous learning performance.

This paper presents the first multi-modal dataset designed to detect abusive expressions on social media, incorporating multimedia content such as images and videos. A novel classification model, named UM2H, is introduced to address the challenge. By combining a deep learning framework with a Transformer-based approach, UML2H integrates visual and linguistic information, employing a unified framework for visual and linguistic feature extraction. A notable aspect of UM2H is the incorporation of a novel attention mechanism, which facilitates the integration of a pre-trained language model with a pre-trained visual Transformer. Furthermore, UML2H incorporates a novel regularization technique, which leverages a shared layer to promote knowledge transfer between modalities. Experimental results on a challenge benchmark demonstrate that UM2H achieves state-of-the-art performance, highlighting the model's robustness and the effectiveness of our training strategy.

We investigate network configurations comprised of type-I neurons governed by the conductance model, with neuronal connections determined by random networks of varying architectures. It has been previously established that synchronization patterns within such networks depend heavily on neuron intrinsic frequencies, topological structure, and distribution of synaptic connections. In contrast to past studies, we focus on how the degree distributions of these networks affect their global synchronization, independent of the neuronal intrinsic frequencies. Our analysis reveals that depending on the density of the degree distribution, the network may develop a binomial, heavy-tailed, or bi-modal structure, which in turn influences the network's synchronization behavior. Specifically, binomial and heavy-tailed distributions tend to produce synchronized networks, whereas bi-modal distributions can give rise to multiple peaks in the neuronal firing times. These results are also applicable to more general networks, encompassing neurons with different intrinsic frequencies and type-I neurons, among others.

A software defect is essentially a constraint that forces the system into an undesirable state, but by introducing the opposite constraint, software can be repaired, thereby turning defect mitigation into an alternative constraint to be met. This concept of an opposing software defect is called a 'shadow defect,' and to tackle shadow defect constraints, our approach relies on 'antagonistic patch creation,' where repair candidates that eliminate one defect are checked to ensure they don't introduce the opposing defect. We've developed a technique to automatically generate antagonistic patches and used this to transform five existing program repair tools, specifically applied to four of them to study the relationship between shadow defects and software's functionality. Results indicate that shadow defects frequently occur within functional areas of software and that our antagonistic patch creation method yields significant improvements in repair quality, particularly increasing the percentage of correct single fixes from 22% to 40%.

A data spectrum has been proposed to analyze communication systems with multiple antennas, allowing us to analyze the capability boundaries of feedback-enabled message transmission with reliable communication. In this investigation, focusing on the time-varying multiple-input multiple-output channel, a data spectrum is derived to understand the finite-length communication limit and its relationship with the number of channel samples and message count. Additionally, concepts from information causality are used to develop an upper bound for the data transmission rate.

We have developed a three-dimensional flow examination tool that enables a comprehensive analysis of a nuclear flow's three-dimensional structure, including its radial and longitudinal variations in density and velocity. By employing flow integration techniques, our method determines the Equation-of-State (EOS) of the nucleus, taking into account uncertainties in input parameters. As part of our approach, we have created a three-dimensional nuclear flow simulator that models n-body nuclear flow in a cubic box with open boundaries. Our 3-dimensional flow examination was applied to several different types of asymmetric heavy-ion collisions, specifically at energies of 32 and 320 MeV/nucleon, to investigate the influence of density profiles, boundary conditions, and other input parameters on the Equation-of-State (EOS). Furthermore, our study revealed significant influences of density profiles on various EOS parameters, such as incompressibility and its curvature. Lastly, our proposed 3-dimensional flow examination can be utilized to analyze real-world heavy-ion collision data to extract valuable information about the EOS of a nucleus.

The rapid spread of COVID-19 has caused a significant global crisis, with effective contact tracing being a vital tool for slowing its transmission rate. Recent advancements in deep learning-based CT scan analysis have shown promise in identifying asymptomatic COVID-19 patients early on, thus reducing the need for extensive physical contact testing. However, traditional deep learning models often require extensive data from various hospitals, raising concerns about patient privacy and potential data breaches. To address these issues, an adversarial, federated learning framework has been proposed that leverages local CT scan data while avoiding the need to centralize patient information. Our proposed framework involves two key components: an adaptive CT preprocessing technique and a Bayesian neural network-based CT analysis model. Our evaluation using real-world COVID-19 CT data demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of our framework, showcasing its ability to balance model accuracy and patient privacy.

This paper investigates the potential of using wireless communication systems to support distributed machine learning applications, specifically focusing on training and distributed inference with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). A detailed analysis of inference training is provided, where it is demonstrated that the structure of the Hessian matrix of the loss function can be leveraged to decompose the GNN inference process into parallel computational units. Subsequently, a wireless communication scheme is designed to accommodate this decomposition, minimizing communication overhead. It is shown that when optimal parameters are utilized, the asymptotic communication complexity at the optimal convergence rate scales cubically with the number of GNN layers. Furthermore, the study highlights the trade-off between the number of training samples, the number of GNN layers, the step size, the channel gain, the noise variance, and the Hessian matrix diagonal element, in order to achieve the optimal convergence rate. Experimental results are presented to substantiate these findings.

A Brazilian state's administrative division consists of 245 municipalities, with the province of Goias comprising 138 of these.  This study analyzes data on the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics for Homicide rates in the region from 2002 to 2014, focusing on historical patterns and spatial variations.  It identifies spatial clusters of high and low rates, revealing an initial pattern of high rates in the capital and low rates elsewhere, which later reversed.  Notably, municipalities with low rates in 2002-2004 became dominant with high rates in 2010-2014, while the central area became more homogeneous and stable.  This transformation is attributed to factors such as urbanization, poverty, and public policy interventions.

Machine learning, specifically deep learning, has seen significant advancements, but the fundamental algorithms remain largely unchanged since the 1960s. This work aims to reexamine core machine learning methods and shed new light on their core principles. The paper specifically delves into the fundamental structure of gradient descent, exploring how various sound levels can be applied to suit different learning scenarios. It examines how adaptive gradient descent and adaptive issue resolution can be applied to accelerate these methods. The paper identifies a suitable framework for gradient descent and highlights the limitations of its current forms. To resolve these issues, the paper introduces a generalized gradient descent approach, incorporating sound and issue adaptations. This new method offers a unified framework for understanding various existing machine learning algorithms, including stochastic gradient descent, statistical learning, and reinforcement learning. The paper also showcases the potential for this approach to resolve several long-standing problems in machine learning, such as vanishing gradients, overfitting, and underfitting. The discussion presented in this work is intended to inspire future research and innovation.

The KATRIN experiment has sparked curiosity about the density of neutrino masses, which KIBOX is designed to study. A separate area of investigation is the solar neutrino anomaly, which the IAXO helioscope is intended to address. By using IAXO to study the energy spectrum of $^{8}$B neutrinos, it will be possible to examine the shape of the $^{8}$B spectrum at high energies and the large matter effect oscillation phase. This will allow for a more precise measurement of the solar neutrino spectrum, which is crucial for understanding the structure of the Sun's core.

We identify a new class of self-exciting systems that function without any bias in their drift coefficient. This class encompasses systems with diffusions defined by $|x|^{\alpha}\cos(\alpha x)$ as their drift, where $\alpha$ lies within the range of $(0,1/4)$. Notably, this encompasses the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, and the systems we've identified belong to the category of超几何型. We establish conditions for the extinction of these systems and categorize the geodesics into distinct types, specifically hyperbolic, elliptic, and parabolic. In the case of elliptic geodesics, we demonstrate the existence of invariant measures for the corresponding diffusion systems.

The growth of service robots working alongside humans in the real world has led to a pressing need for robust grasping techniques that can handle everyday objects. To facilitate further advancements, researchers have developed extensive datasets for training and testing robotic grasping algorithms. However, existing datasets are limited by their focus on basic grasping methods like parallel-finger or whole-finger grips, and they lack a diverse range of objects or the ability to simulate complex interactions. To address this issue, we have created a large dataset called DexGraspNet, consisting of over 85,007 diverse grasping interactions between a dexterous robot hand and various objects found in daily life. We propose a fast rendering method to generate training data from a point cloud-based dataset, allowing for efficient simulation of the required interactions. Additionally, we have incorporated physical simulations to create more realistic and diverse grasping scenarios. Notably, DexGraspNet is the largest dexterous grasp dataset available to date, and it has been made publicly accessible for research purposes.

This article presents an advanced MRI sequence design, a turbo spin-echo sequence, that enables high-resolution, artifact-free 3D body imaging during free-breathing.  This sequence was combined with a multi-channel body coil and a radiofrequency pulse-powered device to facilitate fast imaging, allowing for a detailed scan of the abdomen and chest area.  In the study, two volunteers and 14 patients underwent scanning, and the resulting images were compared to those obtained using a standard sequence.  By optimizing the turbo spin-echo sequence, it was possible to achieve a significant reduction in imaging time, resulting in an acceptable image quality, even at a relatively low signal-to-noise ratio.  Notably, this optimized sequence was able to detect small lesions, approximately 5 mm in size, and provided superior anatomical detail, including a clearer depiction of a lesion located at the edge of the liver, when compared to the standard sequence.  Overall, this research demonstrates the feasibility of acquiring high-quality, free-breathing MRI scans, including those of the body, using a modified turbo spin-echo sequence, and highlights its potential for further development and clinical application.

Model compression is becoming increasingly crucial for cutting down the costs of deploying deep learning models. Model compression techniques like pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation have shown great potential. Among these methods, knowledge distillation stands out as the simplest to use. However, current knowledge distillation methods face several challenges, including the need for extensive trial and error to find suitable distillation pairs, which is time-consuming and labor-intensive. To address these issues, we introduce InDistill, a novel knowledge distillation method that leverages the model's own internal structure to identify suitable distillation pairs. InDistill enables the distillation of knowledge from a deep model to shallower models by analyzing the relationships between model layers and their depths. Through experiments, we demonstrate that InDistill outperforms existing knowledge distillation methods and offers a more efficient way to find suitable distillation pairs.

For submersion functions from the plane to the sphere, a precise determination is provided for when their restricted submersion functions to the plane have the same sublevel set topology. This provision relies on a previously established concept, further refined in this context. Building on this discovery, criteria are formulated for a submersion function to represent a specific class of functions characterized by a certain symmetry, derived from a prior classification of plane foliations derived from such functions.

Plant communities in arid and semi-arid regions are particularly susceptible to the impact of non-resident grazing. We developed a mathematical model to simulate the dynamics of vegetation in these areas, accounting for the effects of non-resident grazers. Our model explores how varying levels of non-resident grazing affect key system properties, including the stability of vegetation, its average biomass, and the frequency of drought-induced extinctions. We discovered that increased non-resident grazing leads to increased variability in plant biomass, as well as more severe drought-induced extinctions. Furthermore, our results show that the consequences of non-resident grazing are more pronounced in areas with low rather than high annual rainfall. Our study also examines the influence of other ecological factors, including the role of plant seeds, the size of grazers, and the length of time grazing occurs, on the outcomes of our model. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the impact of non-resident grazing in arid and semi-arid ecosystems, as well as the importance of sustainable grazing practices.

The performance of machine learning algorithms is significantly influenced by their ability to process large datasets efficiently. When the choice of dataset is left to chance or when a learner adapts to the data, these algorithms tend to perform well. However, scenarios in which a human expert selects a relevant subset of the data exist, and these cases require learners capable of accurately modeling such datasets. To account for these varying levels of expertise, a new framework has been developed, which measures how well linear estimators, such as CountSketch, perform when a dataset is chosen either randomly or by an expert. The framework identifies critical parameters that dictate CountSketch's accuracy, including its dimension and the degree to which an expert chooses the data. The results indicate that CountSketch, including dimension-reduced variants, can provide a constant factor approximation of a sketching matrix relevant to Fugotter-Lin-Shamir linear spectral estimation, provided that its dimension is proportional to the randomness of the data plus a parameter related to the distribution of data. The interaction between dataset choice and the condition number of a matrix is also examined, and it's found that certain matrices, despite being well-conditioned, can lead to inaccurate estimations if their relevant data components fall within a small-dimensional subspace that is chosen by an expert.

ipe, a Python-based quantum Monte Carlo program, boasts exceptional flexibility and efficiency, whether utilizing CPU or GPU processing capabilities. This program incorporates several cutting-edge algorithms for AFQMC, including two innovative GPU acceleration techniques along with additional features such as fast image elimination and biased sampling. Our research showcases peaking performance of up to 1.2 Gbps with m100d GPUs for the U2s system, demonstrating the robustness of ipie even in the presence of parameter optimization. This program is easily accessible through a comprehensive user-friendly interface and an intuitive design, while supporting a wide range of features, including complex orbital basis sets, stochastic estimators, and more. Furthermore, ipie can be seamlessly integrated with external density functional theory programs, allowing for the application of on-the-fly importance sampling based on a Kohn-Sham formalism.

This study explores the application of quantum key distribution in financial transactions, building on its initial discovery in the realm of cryptography, and proposes a Penge Prisoner's Dilemma scenario to examine its implications for transactions. Moreover, this research is supplemented by data from quantum KDDuKE, a quantum-enhanced knowledge graph, which has garnered attention in AI circles. Utilizing the IBM Qiskit framework on a quantum cloud platform, simulations have been conducted, which this paper seeks to clarify and interpret.

Selling an item via a broker, such as eBay, incurs additional costs, but can be advantageous when buyers are scarce. Brokers facilitate transactions by providing a centralized platform for selling, though they charge a commission for their services. In our study, we investigate a seller's optimal strategy for choosing between traditional and broker-assisted sales, given that broker-assisted sales have higher selling costs but potentially larger seller prices and increased demand. The research demonstrates that, despite the higher selling costs, a seller maximizes income by utilizing broker-assisted sales when demand or price sensitivity to costs varies. Our model's assumptions are then relaxed, and the analysis is extended to accommodate more complex scenarios, including multiple price and cost combinations and probabilistic demand functions.

To generate abstractive summaries, modern models rely on creating template-based reductions of input text by reducing it to a set of predefined, generic labels called entity prompts. Research has shown that text planning models, which efficiently transform prompts into summaries, can be used in conjunction with active learning strategies to adaptively select the most representative paragraphs for condensing entire documents. However, acquiring a diverse set of prompts is a labor-intensive process. This study proposes a method for automatically learning prompt sets by repurposing existing pluralization backtranslation techniques, thereby significantly broadening the range of available prompt sets and notably improving their diversity. We then investigate whether these automatically acquired prompt sets can be used effectively in text summarization tasks. Our results reveal that not only do the automatically acquired prompt sets rival the diversity of human-designed sets, but also that summaries generated using these sets demonstrate enhanced quality and coherence when generated by data-driven summarization models, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmark summarization datasets.

This paper examines differentiability in $n$-dimensional space, particularly focusing on the implications of differentiability in $n-1$-dimensional subspaces, and develops necessary mathematical tools and criteria to draw a conclusion. Ultimately, the findings are applied to analyze the differentiability of Dirichlet's function based on the known non-differentiability of its 1-dimensional component.

Researchers have established a connection between speech rate synchronization and social bonding in face-to-face interactions. However, the current understanding is based on observations made in controlled settings. This research aims to address the limitations of existing studies by developing a more accurate and adaptable model for analyzing speech rate synchronization in real-world conversations. The evaluation of the new model is conducted through both experimental and practical applications. Notably, when tested in an experimental setting, it is found that our new model outperforms previous methods in distinguishing between meaningful rate synchronization and random patterns. Moreover, our model is being utilized in a practical application to automatically assess and compare the speech rates of agents engaged in a simulation of a clinical interview.

A recent study by the second author and his colleague, along with Qureshi, has led to the definition of a unifying framework for unitary quantum logic, denoted as the unitary lambda-calculus. This development has paved the way for the creation of interactive quantum programming models that incorporate measurement, conditionals, loops, and function definitions within the quantum domain. Building upon the insights of the aforementioned study, we present the quantum manipulation framework in the unitary sphere (QMS), which draws inspiration from a foundational model developed by Blyth, Plotkin, and Rego. This framework integrates the core principles of interactive quantum programming, such as Lambda S1, along with the capabilities of recursive functions modeled through the categorical interpretation of the unitary sphere. This integration has given rise to the development of QMS, which serves as the foundational element of a comprehensive quantum programming language.

A new approach to solving the Toricale problem in glaciology is proposed, which is formulated as a semicoercive Stokes variational inequality on a fixed boundary. This inequality describes the movement of an ice sheet that is trapped by a tunnel, and its solution is influenced by a time-varying parameter $\lambda$. This parameter represents the boundary's position, which is determined by balancing a pressure term and an external force. By leveraging properties of the operator involved, including its coercivity in a specific cone, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the problem's solution and derive its regularity. Furthermore, an error analysis of a finite element approximation is presented, along with a priori estimates that ensure a discrete version of the underlying estimates holds, thereby guaranteeing optimal and stable convergence.

A cutting-edge dataset, known as DUVET, is presented, which was generated using a high-resolution ALMA telescope to study a peculiar galaxy known as SDSS133415, located in the direction of the Virgo cluster. This peculiar galaxy, classified as an early-type starburst, is characterized by a strikingly bright and compact core, surrounded by regions of intense molecular gas emission. In contrast to typical galaxies, these gas emissions are observed to be smaller than corresponding ionized gas, and are concentrated towards the core, displaying a peculiar rotation pattern. Detailed analysis reveals a striking relationship between gas velocity and metallicity, which is consistent with an outflow originating from the core. This outflow is estimated to have a mass outflow rate of approximately 1000 solar masses per year, significantly exceeding the rate of the underlying star formation. This suggests that the outflow is capable of regulating the rate of the underlying star formation, which is an important control mechanism in the evolution of galaxies.

Our research examines the influence of initial event geometry on the triangular flow $v_3$ through the multiphase transport (AMPT) model. We investigate two collision systems, Au+Au and Cu+Cu, and analyze how using full or mixed initial states affects $v_3$ in mixed initial states, including the role of pre-hadronization stages. We find that in both collision systems, $v_3$ is not significantly affected by initial geometry and that hadronization via a parton-based process (parton hadronization) leads to a decrease in $v_3$ compared to AMPT model results, thereby indicating that parton development and $v_3$ are inversely related.

This research introduces the concept of SimSura, a novel robotic structure composed of multiple interconnected robots that operate simultaneously to build a single, unified framework. Each robot in the configuration functions independently, allowing for the possibility of implementing diverse motion strategies. A primary objective of the proposed approach is to expedite construction time by utilizing multiple robots to achieve a task in a shorter duration. A second goal involves optimizing robot selection to reduce the overall task execution time. A numerical analysis of the SimSura method demonstrates its effectiveness by showing a significant reduction in construction time compared to the traditional sequential approach.

We conducted experiments on a monitor-based depth assessment task, where we evaluated its role in the pre-training of semantic segmentation models. Although monitor-based task formulations have yielded successful pre-training for semantic segmentation, we discovered this task's pre-training does not necessarily lead to superior performance. Instead, we proposed an innovative approach that combines both monitor-based assessment and segmentation tasks to improve the results. Furthermore, our experiment results indicate that this combined task formulation not only accelerates training convergence but also enhances final performance.

A function's Bohr radius is referred to as the largest possible value, called the Bohr radius of the function's class, when it meets certain conditions beyond the unit disk. This research aims to identify the exact upper limit of this radius, referred to as the sharp Bohr exponent, for a specific type of mapping known as starlike log-harmonic mappings, particularly within the unit disk. Moreover, this study seeks to rephrase the main result in terms of the class of parametric harmonic mappings.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is often employed, but traditional methods for estimating its confidence intervals are limited. Only two methods exist, which suffer from inaccuracies such as bias or inefficiency. This research aims to address these limitations by presenting simple alternatives, including intervals based on asymptotic normality, the bootstrap, and a continuity correction. Furthermore, a higher-order asymptotic approximation has been developed using Edgeworth and saddlepoint approximations, a higher-order asymptotic approximation using Edgeworth and saddlepoint approximations.

The integration of Edge Intelligence (EI) into vehicle networks is poised to significantly enhance the functional capabilities of connected vehicles. By incorporating Edge Intelligence nodes (ENs) into the network, collective learning algorithms such as Federated Learning (FL) enable models to be trained more effectively and efficiently, utilizing patient data and vehicle video feeds while safeguarding user privacy. Nevertheless, the centralization of sensitive information in the network raises concerns regarding user privacy. This study proposes a unified framework for protecting user data shared with the central server, known as Privacy-Protecting Edge Intelligence (PEI). This framework is composed of three sub-categories: pre, post, and hybrid data protection methods. Our research focuses on evaluating the performance of hybrid schemes, consisting of pre and post, data protection methods. Our findings indicate that combining robust encryption and distillation-based privacy mechanisms offers an optimal balance between privacy and performance metrics. Our proposed PEI framework is expected to contribute to the development of a secure and reliable EI system for vehicular networks, thereby supporting the deployment of successful and resilient smart transportation infrastructure.
This paper introduces a novel method for creating a diverse range of 2D surfaces based on the Euler top model, encompassing all possible topological structures.

This research focuses on the stabilization effect resulting from mutualism between a predator and its prey, governed by the Holling-Tanner model. We investigate the interaction between the Holling-Tanner type III response and the Allee effect to establish that the coexistence equilibrium in the Holling-Tanner model can be destabilized by strong Allee effects in prey populations, thereby prompting an evolution towards mutualism and stabilizing coexistence. Moreover, our analysis examines the stability of coexistence in the Holling-Tanner model with strong Allee effects and weak predation on zero-prey populations, categorizing the Allee strength into low and high thresholds. Within the low Allee strength range, we confirm that stability transitions occur through Hopf bifurcation, whereas our analysis of the high Allee strength scenario reveals that stability transitions occur through a more complex zero-current manifold.

Our earlier research on the comprehensive pivot method for solving linear programming problems introduced the concept of the aspect pivot simplex method, along with an iterative algorithm, all of which are nameless and considered heuristics. This continues our previous discussion, where we revisit the method, the iteration technique and the associated convergence results. This time, the proof focuses on staying within the feasible solution space using the smallest reduction, ultimately resulting in a theoretically bounded error for any given problem, although the risk of cycling remains possible.

We provide a concrete representation for the NK1 module of Bak's modular group $\K_1(R)$ for a commutative ring $R$ with a graded structure, utilizing relations of degree one, and verified with a concrete example.

This paper examines the impact of gluon and photon virtuality on the precise extraction of the $t$ mass, particularly in the context of the most frequently observed $tt$ event, the $t\bar{t}$ jet occurrence. Our analysis reveals that considering the effects of virtuality on external legs does not significantly impact the extraction of the $t$ mass when using the $m_{C}$ mass definition, and this influence is even less pronounced with other projection methods or the pole mass. However, this does not imply that higher-order corrections are negligible, and our study indicates that accounting for off-shell contributions is essential for the accurate determination of the $t$ mass in the $t\bar{t}$ jet occurrence.

This study investigates the use of the latest vision transformer architecture, known as ViT, for the anti-spoofing detection task. Our research evaluates the performance of ViT in both zero-shot and few-shot learning settings. A pre-trained ViT model is tested with the ASL-IoS platform, and the results indicate that ViT is capable of achieving top-tier performance in few-shot learning. However, when it comes to zero-shot learning, the model is found to be less effective, and its performance is hindered by its tendency to rely on general image characteristics rather than specific user identities. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel ensemble method called RandomCrop, which involves combining multiple random cropped versions of the original image to generate a composite representation. Our experiments reveal that this ensemble approach significantly improves the performance of ViT, leading to substantial reductions in the Equal Error Rate (EER) for both partial and full ASL-IOS platforms.

Self-driving vehicles rely on in-depth analysis and precise decision-making, which necessitates examining an extensive array of variables. The inherent intricacy of these tasks poses challenges to traditional machine learning methods, which typically depend on problem segmentation and feature extraction. In response, researchers have turned to deep reinforcement learning, a more advanced approach capable of handling complex problems through iterative refinement. In this study, we have developed a deep reinforcement learning model for autonomous vehicles, incorporating a comprehensive simulation framework to facilitate the training of this model. The results demonstrate the efficacy of our solution, which has also been successfully applied to a simulated vehicle.

To enhance execution efficiency, a novel asynchronous parallel algorithm for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms has been proposed. This algorithm addresses a critical drawback by eliminating dependency on a generation for operator application. To this end, a customized frequency-oriented parent selection mechanism is introduced to counter the negative impact of evaluation time bias that arises from asynchronous parallel processing. This mechanism designates evaluation frequencies to operators to regulate their execution rates. By utilizing a generational counter to track function evaluations for each solution, bias can be mitigated. The algorithm's efficacy was validated through comparison with a parallel variant of NSGA-III on problems of varying complexity and under different population sizes using the 100-run rule.

The recent discovery of exoplanets through gravitational microlensing has led to a new method called "verification" to confirm their existence. Observations of an event, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, revealed the presence of a cold, 3.7 Earth-radius planet orbiting a cool star at 5.2 AU. Two ALOHA and Keck AO-assisted observations of the microlensing event allowed for a detailed analysis of the light curve, confirming the mass ratio of the planet and star at 0.00296. Further analysis of the data, including image modeling and light curve fitting, revealed the orbital radius of the planet and its cold temperature of 100 K. This discovery is an important addition to the field of exoplanets, as it expands the range of verified exoplanets and provides a new target for direct imaging.

A general method to approach the Markovian approximation of a quantum system interacting with a bath at a specific frequency is developed. This method yields a series of corrections to the Markovian Lindblad master equation, offering a reliable expansion in scenarios where the oscillation frequency is substantially greater than the system-bath coupling. As an example, the spin-boson model is utilized to demonstrate the derivation of the first two corrections to the Lindblad equation, overcoming a longstanding barrier in obtaining a formal expression for this issue. These corrections are verified through comparison with a numerical Chirped Redfield equation. This research presents an enhanced understanding of quantum Markovian approximation and facilitates the creation of high-fidelity quantum devices.

The rare-earth-based intermetallic compounds, specifically CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ with varying concentrations between 0.15 and 0.9, were examined using neutron scattering to study their magnetic phases. It's been established that both edge-sharing and vertex-sharing antiferromagnetic phases coexist in CePd and can be depolarized due to solidification under specific growth conditions. Depolarization is also observed in samples where order is established, indicating that perfect polarization is not achievable. To rectify this, incorporating a spin filter in the small-angle neutron scattering setup is proposed to eliminate depolarization effects.

A comprehensive examination of 21 cm line self-absorbed features in the vicinity of G176.51+00.20, a significant high-mass star-forming area, has been conducted. The observed features are interpreted as evidence of dense, neutral hydrogen clouds situated in front of the background source. Data collected from the Arecibo Observatory reveal 17 such features, while the 20 cm wavelength observations from the Nançay Radio Telescope show additional characteristics. The absence of thermal emission from these features suggests they are located within the high-mass star-forming area, implying that the entire region is embedded within a larger, dense, neutral hydrogen cloud. The observed features are interpreted as a visual representation of the complex environment surrounding G176.51+00.20.

The $\beta$-shift is a type of subshift that is closely related to $\beta$-expansion, a concept in number theory. We explore the connection between two previously defined categories of $\beta$-shifts, namely avaricious and intermediate $\beta$-shifts, by showing that every intermediate $\beta$-shift can be considered a subset of avaricious ones. This relationship is rooted in the growth rate of the number of distinct digits in a given length within these intermediate $\beta$-shifts, which can be characterized by a specific function involving the number of distinct digits and the length of the words.

Dedicated to finding the CP-violating angle phi s in Bs to J/psi pi plus pi minus decays, the LHCb experiment examined data collected from proton-proton collisions at the LHC, spanning 2011 to 2012. With a data set of 3 times 10^17 nb^-1, researchers discovered a non-zero value for sin phi s, significantly deviating from the expected result under the Standard Model. Furthermore, a non-zero phi phi prime was detected, differing significantly from zero based on both likelihood and chi squared tests.

This study investigates an ensemble of domain transfer techniques that utilize deep neural networks. The research encompasses one source domain and 10 target domains, where a total of 10 one-way transfers were evaluated. The deep neural networks examined include AlexNet, VGG16, and ResNet50. As anticipated, the results show that supervision in both the source and target domains yields the best domain transfer outcomes. However, contrary to expectations, un supervised domain transfer also performs competitively. The study further reveals that the choice of base DNN and target domain has a substantial impact on domain transfer performance. The research ultimately recommends that, given the availability of unlabeled data, a distance-based approach is a viable option for adapting models with limited labeled data.

Given a finite field $\mathbb F_q$ and two points in the plane with coordinates from $\mathbb F_q$, this research focuses on counting the number of lines and curves that pass through these two points. Specifically, for planes over finite fields, an exact formula is derived for the number of straight lines and vertical lines. Additionally, certain conditions are provided for the count of slanted lines. Moreover, certain polynomial properties over finite fields are listed in relation to the number of lines of a certain slope passing through two given points. Lastly, certain curves and functions, including conics, the Arnold's example of word-submap, and the inverse of a linear function, are examined under specific conditions for the count of lines and curves that pass through two given points.
This research paper explores the application of geometry in geology through the examination of triangular triangles within a triangular lattice structure.

This paper introduces the Parameterized Interpreter, a novel approach to graph neural networks that separates the architecture design from the training process by using an abstract instruction set. Like a computer, it consists of registers and stacks, but instead of a fixed set of operations, it incorporates dynamic instructions based on the graph structure. By allowing for arbitrary storage and manipulation of node features, users can now tailor GNN architectures specifically to the needs of each task. We demonstrate the Parameterized Interpreter's versatility by adapting it to existing GCT and GSC networks, achieving significant improvements in node classification tasks on the Cora and Citeseer networks, specifically a 1.8% and 1.6% boost in accuracy respectively. Furthermore, our ablation studies highlight the Parameterized Interpreter's ability to learn both effective control flow and node feature representations, representing the first instance of this happening simultaneously in a GNN context.

We conducted an examination of visible substructures within four Coma cluster candidates, including RXCJ0232.2-4420, by analyzing archival X-ray data from XMM-Newton. For each candidate, we established a 2D velocity distribution using [FeXXI] emission lines and identified X-ray substructures by employing a wavelet decomposition technique. In the case of RXCJ0232.2-4420, our analysis revealed the presence of two X-ray emitting substructures, with the primary one characterized by a redshift of 0.033 and the secondary one by a redshift of 0.034. Additionally, we confirmed the X-ray substructure in RXCJ0232.2-4420 through optical substructure detection. To further investigate the nature of RXCJ0232.2-4420, we analyzed the 2D X-ray surface brightness profile, temperature map, and redshift distribution, revealing that the X-ray substructures are not aligned with the redshift distribution and possibly represent infalling galaxies rather than a single cluster.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Module (LMM), a memory-enhanced transformer variant, has shown promising performance on various tasks, including language modeling and translation. However, the training of LMM, much like the Transformer and other deep neural networks, is memory-intensive and benefits from a parallel computing approach to optimize its memory usage. A key factor in parallelizing deep neural networks is the accumulation of reduction operations, which can lead to memory errors and have been addressed in the Transformer through the use of a separate GPU for softmax. This paper presents a more efficient parallelization approach for LMM, which eliminates the need for an additional GPU and instead achieves a more compact design by a factor of four, while also improving the efficiency of softmax computation, reducing data transfers, and minimizing memory requirements for the memento matrix.

This review outlines the experimental searches for the Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP), a hypothesized dark matter particle, focusing on recent search results and technical methods of three main experiment types: direct detection, indirect detection, and collider searches. An examination of WIMPs beyond the traditional Supersymmetric framework is also included.

A language-based game known as the naming game explores how languages develop, spread, and interact. In this study, we investigate the effect of agents migrating between communities on the character of resulting languages. We examine two scenarios: one where a language is entirely transferred when an agent migrates, and another where agents retain multiple words after migration. Our analysis reveals that requiring both communities to transfer a language is not necessary for language convergence when communities are small, but it becomes essential for larger communities. Conversely, the gradual process of agents adopting multiple words during migration facilitates language convergence by allowing the transfer of a limited number of key terms.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly used to solve partial differential equations, particularly in complex situations that cannot be addressed using analytical or traditional numerical methods. Despite their potential, PINNs face challenges, particularly when trained with high-performance platforms like GPUs, due to issues such as inefficient sample usage and suboptimal convergence. These problems are largely attributed to the bias towards simple functions exhibited by PINNs during training, a phenomenon that can be mitigated to some extent through the use of gradient momentum. By mitigating this spectral bias, researchers can improve the efficiency of PINNs on GPU platforms and achieve better results in solving complex PDEs, particularly in high-dimensional settings where gradient momentum can accelerate convergence and achieve a better balance between accuracy and computational cost compared to standard PINNs.

This study builds upon a previous paper by \cite{GK20}, which examined a system of two linked d'Alembert equations. That study concluded that a particular type of boundary control could make the solution decay at an optimal rate of $\frac{1}{t}$. The current paper further develops these findings by exploring what occurs when the second equation is modified to a Kelvin-Voigt equation, and the boundary conditions are altered accordingly. The results show that even with this modification, a boundary control leads to logarithmic decay of the solution, at an optimal rate.

Model-based reinforcement learning methods build a simulation of the environment to find an optimal model first, then use it to find the best policy. In our study, we create a new method called XMH, designed to tackle large-scale Reinforcement Learning problems. This technique makes a modular model that learns from interactions with the environment and uses it to plan the best policy. The model's structure is based on rules derived from induction, allowing it to be easily read and understood. As a result, our method can learn and adapt complex behaviors, breaking them down into smaller, manageable parts, which allows for efficient computation. In experiments, we compared XMH to two other approaches, Deep Reinforcement Learning and EXMH, and found that our method outperforms them when dealing with large-scale problems.

We investigated the nonreversible nature of a two-level quantum system under continuous optical observation, which differs from the quantum Zeno effect and arises from a balance between relaxation rates and observation strength. This effect is not the result of frequent quantum system states freezing due to observation, but rather results from a balance between relaxation rates and observation strength. Furthermore, a theoretical model accurately replicates the effect and suggests potential applications in developing quantum memory and describing irreversible classical phenomena.

We develop a variant of the Fenton inequality for the sum of translated functions within the $L^p$ space framework. This variant incorporates a parameter $\alpha$ and its nature depends on the value of $\alpha$: for $\alpha\geq 1$, the inequality holds a minimum, while for $\alpha\in (0,1)$, it holds a maximum. The approach involves the application of the minimum and maximum modulus principles to the complex extension of the sum function. Furthermore, we identify functions that optimally embody this inequality by minimizing or maximizing at every point in the $n$-dimensional space.

The behavior of $^6$Li under extreme conditions has been thoroughly examined through a quantum mechanical framework incorporating a Hamiltonian that integrates a potential containing the Gogny interaction, which is composed of Gaussian terms. This numerical study, which also considers an effective mass correction, demonstrates that a particular set of parameters from the Gogony interaction, paired with a specific adjustment factor, yields the most accurate results, accurately replicating the binding energy of the $^6$Li nucleus, spin-up and spin-down ionization energies, and quadrupole deformation. Additionally, this investigation investigates how to construct a realistic optical model for $^6$Li, examining the effects of parameter combinations on nuclear properties, such as ionization energies, deformation, and single-particle energies. Furthermore, this research explores the potential applications of $^6$Li as a target for detecting dark matter via spin-dependent interactions, with a particular focus on the role played by deformation in these processes.

Blind Image Restoration (BIR) focuses on restoring a degraded image when only the blurred image and the blur parameters are known. A major challenge inBIR lies in overcoming the non-uniqueness of its solution due to an inherent scale ambiguity, which poses difficulties for machine learning methods. To address this issue, a pre-training approach has been proposed, where a neural network is initially trained on synthetic, blurred images and fine-tuned using the target, colorful, non-uniquely blurred video frames. To improve the quality of the scaling-ambiguous frames, a loss function incorporating a fixed-scale prior derived from natural image statistics is introduced. Furthermore, a method of generating this prior from individual frames is proposed. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through comparisons with the state-of-the-art algorithms.

This paper introduces and investigates two novel types of associative nonuniform Yang-Baxter equations, which serve as localized two-dimensional versions of adS-type and ps-type nonuniform classical Yang-Baxter equations. The study demonstrates that solutions to the two equations can be effectively converted into one another, thereby allowing the adS-type equation to be resolved through the well-known methods applicable to ps-type equations. This discovery facilitates the creation of solutions to the associative nonuniform Yang-Baxter equation in various algebraic contexts. Furthermore, specific solutions are presented for several key algebras. Notably, certain solutions to this equation are shown to possess a distinct symmetry property.

Formal verification offers a high degree of accuracy in confirming that software operates as specified, yet it suffers from two significant drawbacks: the intricate nature of its formal syntax and the arduous process of conducting manual proof checks using specialized tools. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces an approach that extracts logical statements from everyday language, employing natural language to describe expected outcomes, and translates these statements into a form that proof assistants can understand. We propose a proof system, called Natural Hoare Logic, which integrates existing proof strategies with new rules tailored for software that loops, and extracts logical statements from its proof flow. Our goal is to utilize existing proof strategies, particularly those related to software verification, to streamline the verification process. We demonstrate the feasibility of this method by integrating it with the Coq proof assistant, and perform a preliminary assessment of the effectiveness of our approach through a case study involving the verification of a GPS tracking application.

The Canopus consensus protocol, known for its low-latency and Byzantine tolerance, is an enhancement of the PBFT protocol, which reduces the need for costly PoW operations. However, the initial version of Canopus is susceptible to failures and attacks when the primary node is faulty or compromised, which can lead to delays in consensus, especially in networks where the distance between nodes varies significantly. To address these limitations, the RCanopus protocol has been developed, incorporating solutions inspired by the Resilient PBFT and BFT-Safety protocols, which allow the system to transition to a backup primary node and adjust its quorum thresholds, respectively, without incurring additional delays or compromising the system's overall efficiency. Our analysis and simulations demonstrate that RCanopus offers improved resilience and performance compared to Canopus and other protocols such as Tendermint and BFT-Safety, especially in real-world networks with diverse node locations.

Our research investigates the effect of cholesterol on the mechanical properties of lipid membranes, specifically the DPPC-DPPS membrane. To achieve this, we employ molecular dynamics simulations and compare the results of different models: all-atom, coarse-grained, and coarse-grained simulations with enhanced boundary conditions. The simulation times range from nanoseconds to microseconds. We calculate the bending modulus using two methods: eigenmode analysis of undulating membranes and a stress fluctuation method based on the Helfrich model. Our analysis reveals that the DG/CG model is more effective in recovering the bending modulus compared to the eigenmode analysis. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the DG/CG method can efficiently accelerate eigenmode analysis, making it a valuable tool for studying lipid membranes. Finally, our research validates the accuracy of the CG model in predicting the mechanical properties of lipid membranes, specifically in the case of the bending modulus.

We re-examine the loop quantum gravity approach to cosmology, specifically the modified Friedmann equations, and trace back to their origins in the ADM Hamiltonian, taking into account holonomy corrections. By applying this modified Hamiltonian to the Lorentzian distance between trajectories, we find that the quantum correction can be interpreted as a non-local metric effect, which, in turn, leads to an asymptotic linearity that recovers the original quantum correction.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 high-energy cosmic rays detected during the first part of its second run. This catalog includes data on 94 extremely energetic particles with energies above $5.8\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{eV}$ and five particles in the energy range between $5.0\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $5.8\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{eV}$. This catalog serves as a comprehensive reference for high-energy cosmic ray research.

Incorporating uncertainty assessment into deep neural networks is a crucial task.
This study introduces BayesOD, a Bayesian method for estimating uncertainty in object detection.
BayesOD combines Monte Carlo Dropout and stochastic depth as techniques for creating probabilistic object detection networks, and it evaluates performance and uncertainty using mean average precision and average deviation of standard deviation, respectively.
Through rigorous experimentation on key datasets, BayesOD achieved notable success, and it demonstrated significant potential for applications such as reliability and risk management.

This paper presents an approach to predicting traffic predictions based on traffic flow segments. The proposed method involves utilizing traffic flow segment graphs, which are then fed into a graph convolutional autoencoder to forecast traffic flow segment graphs in the future. Experimental results demonstrate that traffic flow segments, rather than traffic time series, can be more effectively used for traffic flow prediction.

We build on the rewriting foundation in the Gray class by introducing the concept of confluence. This extension enables us to address a key query raised by Gray: a strict rewriting system with congruence can generate a consistent function symbol mapping to any given signature. This extension also facilitates the application of rewriting techniques in the context of the consistency problem, specifically for systems with associative functions, as an example.

The hippocampus, a critical memory center in the brain, is involved in a range of cognitive functions, including learning, memory, and spatial orientation. Hippocampal damage or dysfunction, however, can lead to epilepsy and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's. To address these issues, researchers have developed automated hippocampal segmentation techniques, but manual annotation remains the standard for verification. To address this challenge, a novel method has been proposed, which partitions the hippocampus into subfields using advanced machine learning algorithms. This method has been tested on a dataset of 100 MRI scans and has shown promising results, with a particular emphasis on Alzheimer's disease diagnosis. By combining multiple deep learning models, the proposed method achieves high accuracy in hippocampal segmentation and may contribute to the development of more precise medical diagnostics.

In multi-particle quantum systems, the EPR paradox arises from the nonlocal correlations between the particles. A measurement on one particle can instantaneously affect the quantum state of the other, even if they are spatially separated. A particular type of influence, called the transversal effect, occurs when measuring a particle's state alters the conditional state of the other without directly interacting with it. We present an experiment demonstrating the transversal effect in two-photon entanglement by measuring the entangled photons' polarization and transmission paths simultaneously, and show that two detectors' counting rates exhibit the nonlocal correlation predicted by quantum mechanics. Furthermore, by violating Bell's inequality, we confirm that the nonlocal correlation outperforms classical physics. Finally, by applying quantum theory to the experiment, we verify the occurrence of the EPR paradox and show that two detected photons exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, and their joint state is described by the Schmidt number, indicating that the photon entanglement is confined to a two-dimensional Hilbert space.

This study utilizes a low-energy particle transport model to simulate particle transport and analyze captured particles near Earth's orbit by means of Monte Carlo simulations. By incorporating a low-energy cutoff in electron and positron transport, we investigate the effects of different energy thresholds on electron and positron capture rates. Our results indicate an inverse relationship between capture rates and energy limits, with captured particles exhibiting both trapped and non-trapped characteristics near Earth's orbit. We discover that the Heliospheric Current Sheet significantly influences capture rates, especially at lower energy thresholds, and that solar proton flux has a greater impact on capture rates than solar alpha particle flux, especially at higher energies. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that the capture rates of electrons and positrons are comparable at sub-relativistic speeds, while the capture rates of protons and alpha particles are similar at energy thresholds above 100 MeV. Our research contributes to our understanding of particle transport and captures, particularly at lower energies, and highlights the critical role of the Heliospheric Current Sheet in these processes.

Deep Graph Neural Networks have become a prominent area of research in recent years. This work proposes a comprehensive and structured approach to Deep GNN design, incorporating two key components: (1) a network architecture inspired by the human brain's hierarchical structure, and (2) a topology optimization method focused on local connectivity. We begin by reviewing the fundamental GNN blocks and their functions, and then introduce a novel Deep GNN framework characterized by a hierarchical structure that gradually reduces in size. This framework is designed to efficiently capture information at both global and local levels, and demonstrates superior performance on a range of semi-supervised node classification tasks across various network designs. Moreover, we address the computational challenges associated with large-scale Deep GNN models, and propose a topology optimization approach aimed at minimizing connectivity while preserving performance. We extend this optimization method to accommodate training dynamics, and demonstrate its effectiveness using link importance metrics.

This study introduces the first differentially private solution for low-rank matrix completion. Building on the work of Cohen et al. (2015), a novel differentially private matrix completion approach is developed, utilizing low-rank structure, a combination of sub-Gaussian and heavy-tailed noise, and an optimization problem that minimizes the Huber loss. It is theoretically demonstrated that this algorithm satisfies differentially private conditions. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm that the proposed method is effective, with an extension to weighted matrix completion also presented.

We introduce a physical model for the alignment of dust grains, which explains the extinction, emission, and polarization characteristics of interstellar dust. This is achieved by integrating a grain composition consisting of silicate and carbon-based dust (carbon chains, aromatic hydrocarbons) with a grain size distribution, which explains the observed polarization curves. The alignment of dust grains is attributed to wave-like radiation, which provides an explanation for the variation in alignment of different dust grain sizes. The extinction and polarization characteristics of dust in the interstellar medium are explained by a combination of small dust grains and larger particles, which impact the extinction curve's shape. The alignment of dust grains in the interstellar medium is determined by the interplay between wave-like radiation and the grain's shape, which affects its alignment. The alignment of dust grains in the interstellar medium is also influenced by the interplay between the grain's size and the wavelength of wave-like radiation, which affects its alignment. The alignment of dust grains in the interstellar medium is also affected by the presence of larger particles, which impact the extinction curve's shape. A disk around the low-mass star CIDA 1, located 12.6 parsecs away, contains a massive planet that is forming and interacting with the disk's structure. This planet, with a minimum mass of 10.5 Jupiter masses, is believed to be located at 12.6 AU from the star. The planet's presence significantly alters the disk's structure, creating a gap and a truncated inner disk. The planet's mass and location are estimated using a model that incorporates the planet's interaction with the disk's structure. The planet's mass is consistent with the mass of brown dwarfs, and its formation through the gravitational instability of the disk is a possible explanation. The planet's formation through core accretion is less likely due to the planet's mass and the low mass of the star. In the game of Lights Out, pressing a button on the grid triggers a light-up sequence, including the pressed button and its adjacent cells. The maximum clicks required to illuminate the entire grid is a compelling mathematical inquiry. A full illumination with no repeated light, achievable by the most efficient method, is defined as "dilemma-free." The maximum number of clicks needed to illuminate an $n \times n$ grid that is not subject to repetition is denoted by $f(n)$. The primary objective of this study is to determine the value of $f(n)$ for all possible grid sizes.

Image segmentation is a critical process that has been extensively researched. This study proposes a novel segmentation model based on total variation, incorporating image restoration techniques such as Poisson image editing and non-local means filtering. The model combines these processes to generate segmentations. Our model has been shown to produce superior results with reduced over-segmentation, utilizing an optimized gradient descent algorithm for enhanced performance.

The paper presents a methodical approach to address the challenge of abstracting program behavior, specifically focusing on the interpretation of programs with errors. It acknowledges the complexity of understanding the dynamic between a program's ascending behavior and its descending errors, and proposes a two-step strategy to simplify this process. In the first phase, it outlines a general method for constructing incrementally accurate concrete semantics, thereby facilitating a gradual understanding of program behavior. In the second phase, it introduces decoupling techniques that enable abstracting the flow of concrete semantics, thereby increasing the efficiency of analysis. To illustrate this approach, it employs a simple example of a program with errors and demonstrates how the proposed strategy can be applied to analyze such programs.

A novel class of phonons called topological phonons has been identified,
where a peripheral state exists within the phononic bandgap. Researchers have
found that the phenomenon of physical inversion, which typically involves
electrons, can also be manipulated with light in the case of topological phonons.
To demonstrate this, they have employed infrared laser light to dynamically alter
the phononic band structure in a two-dimensional oxide material and observed the
emergence and disappearance of topological phonons. Additionally, they have
shown that the movement of atoms corresponding to these peripheral phonons
produces sound waves in opposition to one another. This discovery holds great
potential for the development of sophisticated phononic devices utilizing
optoelectronic methods.

An outlier detection algorithm that leverages a metric space is presented, with particular emphasis on high-dimensional data sets where distance computations are impractical. This space-based approach contrasts with dimension-based techniques that make assumptions specific to certain space definitions, thereby limiting their efficacy in addressing real-world problems. Our proposed RAPID method leverages a near-optimal data structure to provide rapid and dependable outcome. In the context of outlier detection, RAPID incorporates the density of neighboring points in the near-optimal graph to efficiently compute anomaly scores. This solution is characterized by its speed in computation, yielding super-linear time complexity and low space requirements. Moreover, RAPID surpasses current state-of-the-art performance levels across multiple real-world datasets, while maintaining computational efficiency.

An atom in its ground state, located near a perfectly reflecting surface, may become excited solely due to an atom's motion when it moves along the perpendicular axis, with no external light source present.  When such excitation occurs, the atom can emit an electromagnetic signal that can be measured by a detector positioned on the opposite side of the surface.  An analytical model has been developed to calculate these outcomes.  It demonstrates that these phenomena occur as long as the atom moves at a non-zero speed and no external light is present, with the process being most pronounced when the atom moves at right angles to the surface.

When training a predictive model on data that's structured like a graph, the favorable outcomes often disproportionately benefit certain groups of connected data points, leading to inherent biases within the model. In this study, we address the concept of fairness within data groups, specifically focusing on fairness applicable to any data structure. We define fairness applicable to any subgraph, known as the localized fairness definition. Our approach involves transforming the original graph into a modified version with adjusted connection strengths, allowing us to ensure that localized fairness constraints are met by the predictive model. We provide both theoretical and computational evidence that this fairness can be achieved by our method, with the associated computational costs being polynomial in nature. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments, which showcase its performance in comparison to existing approaches.

This work aims to develop a kinetic model for reversible enzymatic processes,  
utilizing a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to describe the  
concentration dynamics of all system components (free enzyme, enzyme-substrate,  
enzyme-product, and free substrate and product). A novel iterative technique is  
introduced to find an approximate analytical solution to this system, yielding an  
analytically integrable system that generates an approximate analytical solution  
for any time interval. Subsequently, another iterative approach is proposed to  
determine approximate exact solutions to the kinetic model, where each iteration  
involves solving a linear system of ODEs with increasing complexity. Lastly,  
simulation results demonstrate that both methods yield highly accurate solutions  
for any time period, closely matching the exact solution of the kinetic model.

Recent data from the Large Hadron Collider and its 2016 results for proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV are examined in the context of searches for extra gauge bosons in final states containing one or more jets with significant missing transverse momentum. The analysis includes experiments conducted by the CMS and ATLAS collaborations, with the CMS collaboration focusing on single jet final states with decays into leptons and missing transverse momentum, while the ATLAS collaboration examining pair-produced heavy particles with no leptons in their decay. The CMS collaboration established a 95% confidence level exclusion limit of approximately 2000 GeV for a 4000 GeV resonance decaying into a Z boson and missing transverse momentum, with the MSUSY model being the underlying assumption.
