We develop a fundamental approach to gauge the reliability of theoretical predictions based on the available data. The method utilizes the constraints that theoretical models must be subject to, to set a theoretical minimum for the prediction's accuracy. The accuracy of the predictions can be enhanced by including the full set of theoretical constraints, but this is often not feasible. Instead, we demonstrate that the quality of the predictions can be assessed using the constraints that are actually enforced by the data. The method is then applied to several important predictions in high energy physics: $C_P^2$ for the electroweak sector, the trilinear Higgs coupling, and neutrino mixing angles. The method is also explored to understand the role of individual data points in these scenarios.

We analyze the long-term patterns in complex multi-variable time series that exhibit extreme behavior, such as those that are not consistent with standard statistical models. By proving that certain types of dependent time series behave similarly to specific classes of random dependent time series, our work provides practical methods for estimating key statistical parameters and predicting future time series values. Additionally, our results show how multi-variable time series behavior can be understood through a combination of random time series components and remain robust under the influence of dependent sample data.

Efficient low-density parity-check codes are proposed with explicit decoding algorithms operating in linear time. These codes are capable of achieving optimal rate and linear scaling of translation-invariant belief propagation decoding time. Simulations demonstrate a low average number of message passes for the applied decoding method. A code construction based on graph products is also presented, and a specific instance can be visualized as the graph of a tiling of a 4-hypercube. Furthermore, a variant of this code can be constructed using the Kasteleyn method from a chordal diagram, offering the benefit of having sparser check matrices.

A vertex set S is considered a distance r-controlling set in a graph G if every vertex not in set S is within a distance of r from a vertex in S. The minimum size of such a set is denoted by δ_r(G). This paper investigates the parameters of planar and high-girth graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any planar graph G, the parameter δ_2(G) is at most ⌈|V(G)|/4⌉. Furthermore, we establish that for any r ≥ 3, the δ_r(G) of a high-girth planar graph is O(|V(G)|/r). Additionally, we explore the parameters of high-girth sparse graphs, proving that the δ_2(G) of an infinite family of high-girth sparse graphs with average degree approaching 4 is at most |V(G)|/4.

A theoretical model was developed involving a one-dimensional cluster of atoms that is connected to the environment, which is described as a chain of spins. The purpose of this framework is to study the relationship between defects on the boundary and particles within the system. A specific type of topological structure, known as higher-order topological insulators, is analyzed to discover new relationships between boundaries and bulk properties. A computational model, which is analogous to the quantum cluster spin chain, is derived and used to make accurate predictions, which are verified through numerical simulations. A theoretical analysis was also carried out to study the behavior of the system, which is characterized by localized states on the boundary and exponential decay patterns. A specific type of topological structure, known as second-order topological insulators, is studied in order to discover new patterns of mass-boundary correspondence.

A breakthrough in understanding particle physics is being pursued by the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), aiming to identify new particles and novel dynamics. The search for these new particles is a key focus, as the standard model of particle physics has reached its limits in explaining various experimental findings. The lasso search strategy has been employed to explore a wide range of beyond standard model phenomena, including dark matter and theories such as supersymmetry and extra dimensions. The most promising results so far have been found in the supersymmetric field, where the lasso analysis has provided the most stringent direct limits on certain simplified models to date. This analysis has focused on SUSY scenarios involving the pair production of simplified gluino models decaying into various final states, including bottom quarks, charginos, and neutralinos. The significance of these findings lies in the fact that they have set new limits on the masses of these particles, with implications for the standard model of particle physics.

In scientific fields, large datasets are typically visualized through traditional methods like charts and tables, which require significant user expertise. A new system called Bright Field Neural Visualization, or BFiNeV, streamlines data exploration by performing automatic visualizations. The system generates and refines suitable visualization techniques and compositions based on the given input data, performing all necessary tasks including selection of charts and changes in the visualization. To achieve this, BFiNeV combines two key technologies: a neural network-based visualization selector and a fully automated visualization engine capable of producing and modifying visualizations without further user intervention. A comprehensive evaluation involving expert reviewers demonstrated that BFiNeV successfully chooses appropriate visualization techniques and creates high-quality, informative visualizations. Furthermore, user studies involving 20 participants revealed that using BFiNeV significantly reduced the time required to explore data and improved understanding of the data compared to traditional visualization tools.

This study presents the initial results from the Southern Optical and Infrared Imaging Camera (SOIIC) speckle program at the SOAR telescope in 2021. SOIIC, a recently upgraded device, offers high-resolution speckle and super-resolution imaging capabilities by capturing short-exposure images and combining them using point spread function reconstruction techniques. The SOIIC upgrade, completed in late 2020, includes a high-speed camera and improved optics. A series of 2021 observations, focusing on various binary and multiple star systems, demonstrated the camera's capability to achieve 0.25 arcsecond resolution. A notable achievement is the first high-resolution speckle observations of the binary star HD 147506, revealing a precise separation of 0.252 +/- 0.002 arcseconds and a position angle of 159.0 +/- 2.0 degrees. Additionally, new binary star discoveries and previously known systems, such as HD 147506, HD 147780, and HD 147813, were successfully monitored. A comprehensive speckle binary star catalog, including 17 systems, is presented, along with discussions on future development plans for the SOIIC device.

We've discovered that the heavenly algebras in topological lambda-de Rham mechanics have an associated chiral algebra which is novel and previously unknown. Chiral products within this algebra correspond to the large N limit of Wilson loop correlators, with the respect to the fermionic expansion of lambda-de Rham theory. Furthermore, the kinematic colour-kinematics equivalence found in lambda-de Rham also applies to its chiral algebra, with computations of 3-point correlation functions exhibiting this equivalence. In addition, the chiral algebra exhibits an infinite set of 2-dimensional conformal primary fields that integrate the colour-kinematics duality, representing the large N limit of the lambda-de Rham theory's correlators.

Active regions on the sun display complex dynamic behavior and are known to host various types of solar eruptions. A recent study by the Radio Telescope for Astrophysical research (LOFAR) observed an unusual and distinct pattern of solar piston surges, specifically within a high-frequency band, in an active region that had previously experienced an M-class solar flare. The active region, located at a lower coronal height, was found to exhibit distinct radio burst patterns, differing from those typically associated with faster solar eruptions. A notable series of radio bursts, referred to as Type III bursts, was found to be superimposed upon continuous radio emission, referred to as a glow, which was found to be modulated on a distinct time scale. A notable 'sawtooth' pattern was found to be present within the glow emission, which was found to be indicative of piston surges. A recent investigation, utilizing $e^+e^-\to\gamma\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ and $e^{+}e^{-}\to\tau^{+}\tau^{+}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ processes at a future $e^{-}e^{+}$ collider, proposed the existence of flavour irregularities, potentially linked to new physics beyond the Standard Model. This, combined with the ongoing discrepancy in the $\mu$'s magnetic moment, led us to analyze the potential for the general two Higgs doublet model, the most established Higgs sector extension, to resolve the observed anomalies. We found, through analysis of the proposed flavour irregularities and the $\mu$'s magnetic moment along with $B\to K^*\mu\mu$ process, that the general two Higgs doublet model, despite its complexity and additional constraints, is unable to fully describe the potential new physics phenomena indicated by the $e^+e^-\to\gamma\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ and $e^{+}e^{-}\to\tau^{+}\tau^{+}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ processes.

This study explores the dynamics of stochastic whirlpool formations in fluid rings, represented as Wiener modules with topological ring structures. A specific model is developed using functional probabilistic differential equations, which enables precise descriptions of whirlpool dynamics within the ring's constraint. Key aspects of whirlpool behavior, including its rotation and movement, are examined through this new framework. A fundamental existence and uniqueness theorem is provided to ensure accurate whirlpool dynamics modeling. Additionally, this research examines the implications of introducing an external influence into the ring's environment.

The calculation of reduced density matrices and entanglement measures for specific optical network configurations has been carried out using Gaussian states, providing essential insights into the maximum possible values of entanglement measures. These values can serve as reference points for research into non-Gaussian states, particularly the states generated through boson sampling, offering a framework for analyzing experimental outcomes. Entanglement measurements have significant applications, including quantum key distribution and quantum computing, and our findings can contribute to advancements in these areas.

To determine if a student grasps a concept, educators often analyze their problem-solving process by identifying key behaviors in their work. However, capturing reasoning patterns and their evolution over time proves challenging due to the intricate nature of human behavior and the limitations of existing annotation methods. In this study, we represent temporal sequences of student concepts as dynamic graphs, taking into account the varying lengths of student responses. We then train a sophisticated model to automatically learn these patterns from examples, making it possible to detect patterns indicative of a deep understanding from annotated teacher examples alone. We assess our model's effectiveness by predicting student grades based on their problem-solving patterns. Notably, compared to a baseline model, our approach achieves a significant 12% boost in performance. Our findings demonstrate that this method can effectively capture complex, multi-step concepts, even when data availability is limited.

Recurrent neural networks, particularly autoregressive models, have been widely used in fields like speech recognition and natural language processing. However, the reason why these models are effective has remained unclear. We propose a theoretical framework called the Concealed Markov Process, which explains the utility of recurrent networks in tasks involving partially hidden processes. By analyzing the properties of the CМП, we demonstrate that the most efficient concealed state representations are those that minimize prediction error, often leading to the formation of belief states. Furthermore, we find that the CМП provides an optimal concealed state representation, which is also robust and efficient. We validate the recurrence of the optimal CМП, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of the model.

To ensure accurate video action detection, it's crucial to capture the underlying relationships between an action and the surrounding visual features. Current state-of-the-art methods typically employ a global video feature extractor, but this approach often neglects the intricate local structures within video segments. As a result, the connection between an action and its environment remains incomplete. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach called Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) that leverages the spatial connections between global features and local visual features to identify the contextual relevance of each frame within a video segment. By integrating this innovative method, our model is capable of distinguishing actions based on contextual relevance, leading to improved performance. Our proposed network outperforms state-of-the-art models on multiple benchmarks, including MPII Cooking and Charades-EG, and achieves a remarkable accuracy of 54.2% on the ACTS benchmark. Our source code is available for public use at https://github.com/leojiaqi/GCN.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge brought together a global community of researchers to address an essential task in computer vision: matching pixels between images. Following a successful competition in 2020, the event focused on matching natural images with diverse distortions in 2021, spanning from photographic to video content. A total of 33 entries from 24 researchers across 15 countries were submitted, resulting in significant performance improvements over the previous year. Participants demonstrated substantial gains in metrics, with the best models achieving an average increase of 10-15% across all performance indicators. Building on existing methods, submissions incorporated innovative techniques such as Transformers, self-supervised learning, and gradient-based approaches to enhance image similarity assessment. Four prominent methods were presented, with the top performer utilizing the DIPy deep image pyramids framework, combining Transformer-guided features and self-supervised techniques. The leading method also incorporated self-attention for feature matching, while the second-best approach focused on frequency-domain features and learned similarity metrics. The competitive landscape of image similarity assessment is expected to continue evolving, as highlighted by the advancements made in the 2021 challenge.

This work explores the long-term behavior of one-dimensional parabolic equations on changing domains that experience disturbances and changes in coefficients, specifically degenerating coefficients. To account for boundary disturbances, we consider the case where the boundary moves in a stochastic manner. To prevent the metastability phenomenon, the free energy potential must have a parameter that tends to zero over time, causing the moving boundary to be attracted to a single stable equilibrium position. Additionally, the study investigates how the number of wells in the free energy potential affects the homogenization of the parabolic equation. Furthermore, the research examines the implications of combining moving boundaries, degenerating coefficients, and well formation on the asymptotic behavior of the parabolic equation, ultimately leading to the development of novel mathematical tools for studying these complex systems.

A modified, realistic nuclear force known as the Argonne $v_{14}$ potential was combined with a modified version of the Arndt-Badziag field energy to analyze various properties of the phase. Zschocke's energy correction for the LOCV energy was applied to account for the Pauli principle, and various parameters, such as magnetic field strength, neutron to proton ratio, energy density, and energy per nucleon, were analyzed. A specific range of 10 to 30 times $10^{18}$ Gauss was considered for this phase. A significant increase in the neutron to proton ratio was observed with the application of a stronger magnetic field. Balancing communication efficiency and data confidentiality in Federated Learning (FL) is a significant challenge. The challenge is compounded by differential privacy (DP) constraints, which typically necessitate sending comprehensive updates to the server. To address this, we propose a novel approach, called DP-REC, that significantly reduces communication costs. DP-REC-REC alternates between the server and clients by allowing the server to send restricted exponential family (REC) updates and clients to return REC-based differential private (DP-REC) updates, thus optimizing communication. Furthermore, our approach presents two solutions to the efficiency issue arising from the increased size of REC models. The first involves a compression module, while the second utilizes a server-guided data selection strategy to send only data relevant to the specific REC component being updated. Experimental results validate DP-REC-REC's efficacy, demonstrating its ability to achieve substantial communication savings, particularly when combined with the adaptive selection strategy, while maintaining robust model privacy and generalization.

A recent study of a distant galaxy has provided the first UV data for four of its distant nebulae, including Taurus-Perseus-Auriga. The observations were made using the Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph on a 3.9-meter telescope, and the resulting data revealed detailed features of star-forming regions, including the Orion nebula, which was used as a benchmark for comparison. A variety of emission lines were detected from each region, including C III/N III, O VI, C IV/N IV, and Si III/Mg II, which were attributed to photoionization by ultraviolet radiation from nearby stars, as well as ionization by X-rays and photoevaporation of neutral hydrogen clouds. The Si III/Mg II emission was found to be consistent with photoionization by X-rays, and the observed emission lines provided valuable insights into the physical conditions of these star-forming regions.

Structure preservation is of the utmost importance when extracting tabular data, as it ensures that information can be accurately utilized through appropriate arrangement. Traditional table extraction techniques, however, often fail to convey spatial relationships between cells, thereby compromising the integrity of the data. In this study, a novel approach to PDF table extraction based on Graph Neural Networks is presented. This method involves a graph-based representation of cells, where cell content and visual features are leveraged to facilitate understanding. Notably, a Graph Neural Network model is employed to recognize rows and columns, while a Graph Autoencoder is used to encode the cell content and compress the graph structure. This results in a compact table representation consisting of a set of graph nodes, where node features encapsulate the table's semantic meaning. Experimental evaluations conducted using the 20BillionTables dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in reconstructing table structures, with a precision rate of 84.36%, recall rate of 85.14%, and a mean average precision score of 79.24%.

A multi-phase game of insufficient information involves multiple agents, each participating in a separate and sequential decision-making process. In each round, every agent simultaneously makes a choice based on their private signals, without revealing them to others. This process continues for a predetermined number of rounds. A notable example of such games are repeated 2x2 coordination games with imperfect information. 

These types of games have been analyzed by various scholars, who have explored how equilibrium strategies evolve over time as rounds progress. Our research delves into understanding the underlying patterns of this evolution by introducing a framework that categorizes decision-making rounds into distinct 'cognitive layers'. 

Our 'Cognitive Layers Theorem' reveals that the first round of decision-making is the most intricate, with subsequent rounds becoming increasingly straightforward as rounds progress. Specifically, in a multi-phase 2x2 coordination game with N rounds, we can identify N distinct cognitive layers. 

Our analysis shows that the likelihood of agents being uncertain about the content of their signals increases with each round, until they reach the highest cognitive layer where their confidence is at its peak. Beyond this point, subsequent rounds become simpler, with agents having clearer understandings of their signals and the game's structure. 

Our framework also allows us to re-examine and provide new insights into existing findings related to repeated coordination games, explaining how agents can converge on focal points without direct communication. In Mozambique, the challenge of pinpointing where people reside in unexplored areas hampers effective resource allocation and disaster response efforts. The lack of detailed location data in government surveys is further exacerbated by the absence of individual address information. This study proposes the APES system, an innovative tool designed to provide more precise population estimates by utilizing small survey samples. Through a mock experiment, we demonstrate how APES can significantly enhance accuracy compared to traditional methods, even when accounting for imperfect classification. Our results indicate that a modest sample size can yield substantial improvements over conventional estimation techniques.

In the field of data compression, large datasets are often filtered using a data structure called a membership query filter (MQF), which efficiently determines if specific data items are present within the dataset with minimal memory usage and fast lookup times. A recent advancement in this area, introduced by Behrisch et al. at the 2020 ACM SIGMOD conference, involves a new MQF-based data structure called Estimated Membership Query Filter (EMQF). EMQF achieves its goals by dynamically allocating resources, only storing specific data items confidently within it, and performing fast lookup times. However, EMQF initially had a drawback of potentially containing false positive items. This paper presents a novel approach that rectifies this issue by creating a separate, more precise dataset called the Confidence Set (CS). A simplified version of EMQF, known as EMQF-CS, removes the previous false positive items from the dataset and stores them in CS. EMQF-CS achieves its objectives by containing a predetermined number of dataset items, quickly determining the presence of specific data items, and containing no more than a predetermined number of false positive items. Furthermore, EMQF-CS enables fast determination of the presence of specific data items in the dataset.

The spin of a dimer is restricted to being composed solely of two spinless fermions, resulting in a restricted, classical-like state despite typically displaying quantum characteristics. We propose an experiment involving recombination of atoms to create an unconventional dimers where the spin can take on any value between two integers. The creation process would utilize a multi-step two-photon transition triggered by an inelastic collision between atoms, facilitated by a transient state where an atom transfers its properties to a dimer through a dynamically formed transient state.

A novel, multi-scale Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method is introduced, incorporating a spatial stratification, to simulate complex multi-phase flows involving deformable solids. The strategy integrates solid dynamics with its corresponding time increment, and employs an adaptive accuracy approach, assigning distinct numerical treatments to each phase according to its characteristics. The multi-scale strategy incorporates novel features, including separate time steps and numerical methods, to achieve efficient and accurate simulations. The two-field SPH formulation, optimized for interface resolution, plays a pivotal role in capturing accurate fluid-structure interactions. The presented approach, utilizing an incompressibility formulation, demonstrates its efficacy through a range of multi-phase/ multi-material tests, encompassing both static and dynamic scenarios, to validate its capabilities.

A quantum learning approach is presented, which has both unmonitored and directed implementations, utilizing a scenario where the target function maps random inputs to outputs influenced by instructing parameters. This method is applicable in scenarios including experimental setups and multi-agent environments. Compared to existing quantum algorithms like QLSD, which assume access to an ideal quantum oracle, our unmonitored quantum instruction learning (UNIL) algorithm relaxes this constraint, instead allowing measurements of instructing parameters with inherent noise. This is particularly beneficial for near-term quantum devices where imperfect control is prevalent. Furthermore, our instructing quantum learning algorithm (QIL) demonstrates its efficacy through a simulation involving experimental inputs, which is expected to be a relevant test case for NISQ devices. This research is motivated by the necessity of developing robust quantum algorithms capable of handling realistic measurement uncertainties and providing a clear path for their practical application.

A recently developed neural network, FastPitch, has made it possible to control pitch in human-sounding speech. Despite this progress, current models struggle to maintain high audio quality when pitch is set at highly unnatural rates. In response, we propose an algorithm that can quickly generate waves at any pitch rate while preserving the speaker's original timbre. Our method involves a two-stage process where a learned pitch wave generator is combined with a timbre-preserving pitch shifter. This allows the speaker's timbre to be adjusted to a different pitch without any noticeable change in tone or style. When integrated into FastPitch, our algorithm allows for the creation of speech that sounds like the speaker, but at a different pitch rate. Through a combination of automated and human evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in maintaining high audio quality and flexibility at various pitch rates.

The model 'Hopper' is a new approach designed to tackle the challenge of predicting the movement of geospatial objects over extended time periods, known as spatiotemporal forecasting. This model tackles the issue of reasoning about objects' future locations across multiple time hops, and can be applied to a variety of scenarios such as movement prediction and trajectory analysis. The framework, along with accompanying predictions, is publicly available for replication. Experimental results demonstrate that 'Hopper' significantly outperforms established baselines, including using non-recurrent models, when tested with minimal supervision and without including any domain-specific knowledge. This study aims to set a new standard for object movement prediction models and provides a benchmark for future research.

The $W$ boson mass is a crucial parameter influenced by the fundamental electroweak framework and various higher-order corrections. Precise measurements from the Large Hadron Collider and CERN's direct $W$ boson mass experiment contribute to testing the Standard Model's predictions, including the effects of quantum corrections. The measurements are based on data collected between 2011 and 2018, resulting in a $W$ boson mass of approximately 80.44 GeV with a small margin of error. The findings are consistent with the Standard Model's predictions, but any significant discrepancies in future measurements could indicate the presence of new physics.

The widespread adoption of Telepresence Robot Control (TPRC) applications has been hindered by the lack of research on user experience quality in this area. To address this gap, we conducted the first Interactive User Experience Quality study focused on TPRC. The experiment, which involved 20 participants, was designed to assess the impact of video compression on user experience quality. By comparing different video compression methods, we discovered that perceptible differences in distortion can significantly affect the quality of user experience. To mitigate these differences, we recommend using a video resolution of at least 720p and employing ultra-low latency video compression techniques. The experiment also revealed that interaction latency is a critical factor in determining user experience quality, which can be mitigated by utilizing advanced scheduling algorithms. The study's findings were further supported by the development of a user-friendly survey tool, which allowed participants to evaluate their overall user experience quality. The proposed metric, the Telepresence Robot Experience Model (TREM), was proposed as a potential indicator for TPRC user experience quality.

This study introduces hierarchical regression models through Bayesian models, allowing for more precise parameter estimation by accounting for correlations between parameters across different groups. The model partitions parameters into two levels - a higher-level parameter population and a lower-level parameter distribution, with the group parameters modeled as following a multivariate normal distribution characterized by parameters at the higher level. The study provides detailed Bayesian linear models, including the derivation of the posterior distribution of parameters, along with an introduction to the Bayesian analysis software 'Baysian', specifically highlighting the 'BaysianHLM' module, for conducting Bayesian hierarchical linear models. The research also presents examples illustrating how to calculate the posterior distributions of parameters, along with confidence intervals, incorporating covariates. The accompanying discussion highlights challenges associated with implementing Bayesian models, particularly concerning the derivation of the posterior distributions, and also introduces Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods as a means of approximating the difficult-to-compute posterior distributions. The study also discusses Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling, including the 'BaysianHLM' module's implementation of this technique. The research further includes discussions on convergence diagnostics, such as the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic, as well as approaches for estimating the difficult-to-compute marginal distributions of the model parameters, including Fully Conditional Sampling and Parametric Draws.

To investigate the game of Mafia, a numerical model has been developed to analyze its dynamics. This model's outcome is then compared with observed data in order to gain insight into the game's progression. This study primarily focuses on the two-player scenario in a public setting, a case in which both players are fully aware of each other's identity. By employing a game-theoretical approach, a numerical model has been constructed to evaluate players' strategies, which are primarily based on confidence levels. This confidence is influenced by the accuracy of decisions made during the game. By comparing outcomes from numerical simulations with actual data, a deeper understanding of game dynamics may be achieved. This study primarily focuses on the two-player scenario in a public setting, a case in which both players are fully aware of each other's identity.

A pair of massive planets, located at 5 au from a star, are studied in a 2000 $M_{\odot}$ mass protoplanetary disk. A gas accumulation phase is initiated, where the planets' masses are increased from 2.5 to 3.5 Jupiter masses. This is done by a model that considers the disk's gas density and a pressure wave structure. As the planets grow, a pressure wave develops, and the inner disk's gas is gradually accreted onto the star, causing the planets to undergo a period of rapid mass increase. This process causes the planets to move slightly apart, and they continue to accrete gas from a disk that becomes increasingly asymmetric. As a result, the lighter planets retain a substantial gas disk, while the heavier planets accrete gas from the disk's more concentrated regions. This process causes the planets to become increasingly misaligned, and their orbits become more complex.

A dense array of carbon nanotubes in the form of a thin film possesses unique properties beneficial for photonics, plasmonics, and electronics.  One notable property, electronic intertube transfer, can be manipulated to produce optical phenomena such as the suppression of light.  However, the mechanism behind electronic transfer is still unclear, and a recent study shed new light on this by using phonon-assisted transfer in armchair carbon nanotube films to create an optical dip in the transfer spectrum.  By measuring the optical response of the thin film and analyzing its electronic band structure, researchers confirmed a transfer process involving phonons and phonon momentum.  Furthermore, the researchers demonstrated that this transfer process can be modulated by applying an electric field, indicating the potential for photonics and polaritonic applications based on this phenomenon.

Clustering is a fundamental technique in data mining, but traditional methods struggle with the challenges presented by the high dimensionality of data. The success of a clustering approach is often hindered by the negative effects of high dimensionality, making it crucial to develop effective solutions for handling high-dimensional data. In this context, we propose the Entropy-driven Variable Feature Weighted Fuzzy k-Means (EVFFKM) algorithm, which addresses the issue of feature irrelevance by assigning dynamic weights to individual features. The weights are determined using an entropy-based evaluation, allowing the algorithm to adapt to the importance of each feature. The numerical results demonstrate that the EVFFKM algorithm achieves improved performance, as measured by the partition evaluation criteria and the total error rate, compared to several existing clustering methods.

Mixture-of-experts, a legacy and adaptable machine learning approach, has been adapted to an asynchronous parallel setting known as Mixture-of-Experts (MoEx), which is a widely-used technique. However, the original MoEx algorithm, first proposed in 2017, suffers from a deadlock problem caused by its asynchronous updates, rendering convergence unattainable. This issue has persisted as a major limitation of MoEx, hindering its applications in large-scale distributed systems and impeding research progress. This paper aims to resolve the longstanding MoEx deadlock problem, presenting two new, efficient, and reliable algorithms for continuous and discrete expert models. The proposed algorithms, utilizing a novel exponential moving average, demonstrate reliable convergence to the optimal solution, demonstrating their capacity to outperform existing methods, particularly for time-constrained models, based on theoretical analysis and experimental validation.

Consider a hyperbolic surface of a specific genus accompanied by two special points. A playful contest can be established between two players, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, involving the actions of firing tokens around the surface while adhering to the associated Jacobian constraints. A notable discovery is that when both players have the ability to win, their respective strategies are connected to specific mathematical forms known as Prym forms of an admissible double cover of the surface. Furthermore, cases where one player has no possible winning strategy are also identified.

To assess the impact of global symmetries in quantum gravity, we analyzed recent observations of cosmic birefringence, which indicate that BSM physics could generate a $ \sim 10^{-3} $ anomalous rotation of CMB polarization. Our analysis shows that this phenomenon places a constraint on the scale of any global symmetry breaking. Specifically, our calculations indicate that for $ \mathcal{O}(1)$ coefficients, the global symmetry scale must exceed $ \sim 10^{13} $ GeV. This limit may rule out some models of BSM physics, such as certain dark matter theories and partial fourth generation models. However, this constraint can be relaxed if there is a connection between the birefringence and an axion-like field, which could arise from a spontaneously broken global symmetry. In this case, our analysis suggests that the global symmetry scale should exceed its Planck scale bound by Planck-suppressed operators, which could indicate that global symmetries in quantum gravity are disrupted.

photometry of the globular cluster NGC 4147 using the UVIT onboard the AstroSat.
By utilizing the FUV and NUV filters, we derived the cluster's FUV and NUV
luminosities, as well as its FUV/NUV ratio, across its central regions.
The findings indicate that the FUV/NUV ratio in NGC 4147 is notably lower than
the average for 41 clusters observed by UVIT.
Our analysis of FUV and NUV light profiles reveals that the FUV and NUV light
distributions in NGC 4147 are consistent with King model isophotal shapes up to
approximately 10 cluster core radii.
By employing a maximum likelihood method, we identified the spatial
distributions of FUV and NUV luminous stars within NGC 4147.
Our research identified 107 FUV-luminous and 111 NUV-luminous stars, with
spatial distributions that are largely consistent between the two populations.
Notably, the NUV-luminous population exhibits a 10% excess over the FUV-luminous
population.
