The feeble $b$-principle for smooth sheaves over simplicial schemes was introduced to offer a potential solution to the Mumford conjecture, as proposed by Witten. Building upon this concept, we established the weak Mordell-Lang conjecture for smooth algebraic varieties and smooth group varieties over $\mathbb{G}_m^k$. Additionally, we introduced the principle of effective feasibility and presented examples demonstrating the feasibility or infeasibility of algebraic problems using smooth sheaves, along with a proof of the finiteness of rational points in the context of the weak Mordell-Lang conjecture.

The concept of transferability in deep learning, a key factor in the success of very large models, is often misunderstood due to the lack of clear definitions. This study focuses on the two main notions of transferability: source-target transfer and random-target transfer. These concepts are commonly applied in different evaluation methods but their underpinnings are unclear. This research provides a formal structure to these notions, based on a hierarchical model of tasks, and clarifies that: (i) source-target transfer involves the movement of knowledge across similar tasks, and (i) random-target transfer assesses the level of generalised understanding of the trained task. This understanding is further demonstrated by the development of a metric for transfer performance, known as the transfer metric of similarity. This research finds that the overlap in semantic meaning, or concept overlap, effectively predicts the level of knowledge transfer in both random-target and source-target scenarios. This study provides insights into the mechanisms behind transfer learning and the factors contributing to its success.

In various biological and social systems, the dynamics of information spread are a significant phenomenon. Graph-based models, which represent the information transfer process, are commonly used to study this phenomenon. While most existing research focuses on how network structure influences the speed of information dissemination, we investigate the relationship between network modularity and information spread based on a used-case query model. We reveal that low-modularity networks facilitate rapid information dissemination, whereas high-modularity networks result in slower information transfer. Through analysis of real-world networks, we find that information spread speed is contingent upon the specific propagation process and can vary significantly, even in networks with similar modular structures. We also outline potential extensions of our findings to accommodate different network and query conditions.

For every minimally parabolically stable, horizontally convex, mean curvature flow singularities with a parabolic graph, we demonstrate the existence of unique, radially symmetric, monotone surfaces that are invariant under translations and rotations. These surfaces share similar properties with those found in the self-shrinker case, including the ability to separate and bound the surface from the origin by certain radii. The distinctiveness of these surfaces can be quantified using the Thomas-Yau distinctiveness constant, showing it is finite and scales with a specific power of the distance from the origin. Additionally, we establish bounds on the angles between these surfaces and the radial direction, showing the angle approaches zero as the distance from the origin increases at a specific rate.

A theoretical framework for the perturbation model is presented, which aims to offer a computationally efficient and mathematically sound simulation of electromagnetic wave propagation in complex environments. This model's performance is evaluated through simulations conducted on a synthetic unamplified link scenario. To assess its efficacy, the model's outcomes are contrasted with those produced by a standard full-wave solver. To address the challenge of considerable computational demands associated with the conventional approach, an optimized simulation method based on the perturbation model is developed. This optimized approach involves the identification of key geometric features of the scenario, which are then utilized to derive a set of generalized equations governing wave propagation. The optimized method demonstrates substantial speed improvements, enabling efficient simulations within a reasonable time frame.

Mobile devices are now widely used for mobile app development, with the Google Play Store hosting over 3 million apps. As a result, malware has become a significant threat, posing risks to users' sensitive data and financial security. To counter this, anti-malware tools have been developed to detect and block malicious apps. However, this has led to an arms race between malware and these security tools, in which malware creators have begun employing a novel tactic known as issue-scape evasion assault. In this strategy, malware creators intentionally introduce bugs into their apps to avoid detection by signature-based and machine learning-based anti-malware tools, while still targeting specific mobile platforms. This paper is the first comprehensive review of this phenomenon, analyzing the motivations, characteristics, and strategies behind issue-scape evasion assaults, as well as the impact on the developers and the broader community.

The sheer variety of programming languages and execution environments poses significant challenges when attempting to manage applications, especially as distributed systems become increasingly complex with the introduction of numerous new services and dependencies. To address these issues, our proposal, Ozy, is a distributed orchestration platform that serves as a universal framework for running software, enabling the integration of code written in any programming language and being deployed on any execution environment. By integrating Ozy into existing distributed computing systems, we can streamline the adoption of new technologies and mitigate the drawbacks associated with proprietary platforms. This paper will detail our approach to building universal orchestration, illustrate Ozy's practical applications, and discuss its integration with existing distributed computing platforms.

Our study has identified a new reentrant quantum Hall phase in bilayer graphene, occurring when the inter-landau-level coupling is at a moderate level. This is achieved by employing a realistic Hamiltonian that accounts for the intricate effects of electron-electron repulsion and electron-phonon interactions. A new phase transition is observed, separating an initial reentrant phase from another at higher couplings. This new phase is distinguished by a unique filling fraction of 4.5 and exhibits inhomogeneous states. Furthermore, our research reveals a second-order phase transition with the presence of a critical point. Our findings are consistent with recent experimental results and may be detectable through the analysis of sample hysteresis and the width of the Hall resistance plateau.

This study challenges the notion that the Thakurta metric universally characterizes all non-rotating, electrically charged black holes in an expanding universe. A review of prior research demonstrates that the Thakurta black hole is a unique solution, and the application of the Schwarzschild or Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes is a simplification. A novel approach is presented to determine the horizon radius of the Thakurta black hole, and the comparison of this radius with that of the Schwarzschild and Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes is presented. A significant challenge arises in the use of the LIGO-Virgo constraints on primordial black holes, which are typically characterized by the Schwarzschild black hole. A crucial realization is that these constraints are placed on a specific range of masses, and the use of the Thakurta black hole does not alter the bounds. Consequently, the Thakurta black hole does not modify the LIGO-Virgo constraints on primordial black holes, and the conclusions drawn in [arXiv:1901.07509](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.07509) remain valid.

The process of planet formation involving the accumulation of dust grains that have coagulated into planetesimals is a pivotal stage in the development of planets. The theory of radial drift of solid particles suggests that these grains would be transported by gas from the outer regions of the protoplanetary disk towards the inner regions, where they would be incorporated into the protosun through the process of sublimation. However, observations of protoplanetary disks indicate a discrepancy between the predicted and actual patterns of dust distribution, which is attributed to the effects of gas turbulence and the accumulation of dust rings. This study investigates the mechanisms behind the accumulation of these dust rings, which are thought to be caused by the radial drift of dust grains that are trapped at pressure bumps. The research explores the role of grain-grain collisions in overcoming the radial drift of dust grains and accumulating at pressure bumps, which is an essential step in the formation of planets. The simulations conducted by the researchers reveal that grain-grain collisions can play a crucial role in the accumulation of dust grains at pressure bumps, which is an essential mechanism for planet formation.

From a computational limitations perspective, overparameterized models can significantly reduce the time and resources needed for learning, particularly when utilizing gradient descent methods. This paper investigates a basic learning scenario under such a framework, demonstrating that using a linear model results in exponential learning times using certain adversarially constructed datasets. In contrast, overparameterized neural network models offer substantial improvements, accelerating learning by polynomial factors through the leveraging of nonlinearity, and this acceleration can be quite pronounced without increasing dataset complexity. Additionally, our study explores the relationship between model overparameterization and the applicability of certain theoretical principles like the "double descent" phenomenon and the "lazy training" behavior, and we also address a common assumption regarding the smoothness of loss functions without offering a definitive conclusion.

We expand upon previous work by exhibiting an infinite abelian group that satisfies three specific criteria: it possesses a subgroup with finite index, its quotient by this subgroup is countably infinite, and its unit component is torsion-free. This discovery offers a more comprehensive version of Bohr's structure theorem for locally compact abelian groups, effectively replacing finite quotients with infinite groups having a dense subgroup, while replacing torsion with a group of quotients that is pre-compact when viewed as a quotient of its unit component. The theory is further extended by incorporating new results on the automorphism groups of countable abelian groups and their related structures, as well as the study of almost periodic functions and Bohr compactification in such groups.

The dial-a-ride problem, a variant of the vehicle routing problem, involves optimizing a fleet of vehicles to pick up and transport demand customers from specific starting points to designated ending locations, while minimizing the distance traveled by each vehicle. This research introduces a novel branch-and-trim algorithm to address the issue. Specifically, a Branch-and-Trim algorithm is proposed, incorporating adaptive separation rules to eliminate infeasible customer sequence combinations. Additionally, a branch-and-trim algorithm is developed, allowing for the efficient identification of starting and ending locations of each vehicle route. Extensive computational experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed algorithm, demonstrating significant performance improvements over existing Branch-and-Cut methods, with the latter being less effective and requiring longer computation times. Furthermore, the algorithm's practical applicability is validated through successful real-world deployment, yielding high-quality solutions for actual problems.

This study introduces a multi-modal pretraining method, which is specifically designed for a real-world scenario within the e-commerce domain. We utilize text, image, and video inputs to conduct our pretraining, but this time, we incorporate additional knowledge-based features derived from graphs that are highly relevant to e-commerce. We then fine-tune the model using a large dataset consisting of 10 million negative samples, which is a scenario where no positive updates are present. We evaluate the performance of our approach on a range of e-commerce tasks and demonstrate that it surpasses single-modal and non-domain-agnostic graph-based models. Moreover, our pretraining strategy yields significant improvements when compared to a multi-modal baseline that does not consider domain-agnostic generalization.

A potential condition is often described as a state in which a person may or may not develop a certain disease. Forecasting the progression of such conditions can be challenging, particularly due to the limited availability of diagnostic tests and clinical data. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating knowledge from unlabelled electronic health records using the Deep InfoMax self-supervised learning approach. We compare this approach with traditional methods and full training strategies, utilizing the Australian National Alzheimer's Disease Data Archive's longitudinal data split into progression from stage 1 to 2 and stage 3 to 4 predictions. We explore the effects of incorporating unlabeled data across various settings and find that Deep InfoMax is capable of enhancing the forecasting of both transitions when combined with unsupervised learning on a diverse range of unlabeled clinical records.

Building upon Kripke semantics, a formal method for analyzing computational processes, this research employs a stochastic approach to accommodate variability and unpredictability in computations. Leveraging the flexibility of stochastic bisimulation, our analysis uses a deep recurrent neural network to model computational behavior, facilitating the comparison of language semantics through an interactive, step-by-step process. The proposed system, evaluated on datasets of Java programs, demonstrates effectiveness in detecting and learning program invariants and constraints.

We have developed an approach to enhance the spin-orbit interaction in a correlated metal by utilizing the exchange mechanism, specifically through the incorporation of local f electrons and virtual hopping via neighboring ligands. The mechanism's effectiveness is influenced by parameters including interaction strengths and hole concentrations. The proposed approach's feasibility has been demonstrated through calculations involving the spin-orbit coupling of 5d transition metal iridium's 5d electrons, utilizing embedded f-electrons and hole-doping, yielding a substantial enhancement in spin-orbit interaction.

We investigate the long-term behavior of solutions to the conformal flow in 3-dimensional space. Specifically, we analyze the flow's behavior when it deviates from its equilibrium state, represented by the static solution. By employing inverse metric methods from prior studies, we achieve a global existence result for the flow in 3D. Moreover, we define a Lyapunov functional and demonstrate that the flow solution rapidly approaches a stable, exponentially invariant state. Our work also reveals that the behavior of the flow far from the equilibrium is similar to that of solutions to Laplace's equation outside a sphere, particularly exhibiting exponential decay.

In the field of AI-driven medical imaging, models are often developed and tested using specific datasets, but in practice, they're deployed across a diverse range of hospitals and patient populations. This significant difference in data distributions can lead to unexpected model failures. This study aims to address this gap by developing a reliable method for evaluating AI models across various institutions using limited test data, even when those institutions' demographics are unknown. This involves utilizing an adaptive technique called conformant prediction, which adjusts predictions based on past errors. Our approach simplifies this process by leveraging the accuracy of the AI model itself to create synthetic labels for testing. Using real-world examples from AI breast cancer detection and liver segmentation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in accurately assessing AI performance across diverse hospital settings, with results showing improved accuracy and reduced errors compared to traditional evaluation methods.

A new technique, termed Stiff Base Biasing, has been developed to enhance the modeling of DNA interactions by simulating improved DNA flexibility. Achieving this by modeling the DNA backbone's movement relative to a rigid base, the method has demonstrated significant benefits, including faster convergence and enhanced sampling of key biological processes such as flexible bending and protein interaction-related twisting changes. When compared to traditional simulations, Stiff Base Biasing enabled the efficient exploration of flexible bending and twisting variations, resulting in notable improvements in free energy calculations and overall sampling capabilities. Furthermore, the method's capabilities were successfully applied to the study of an important DNA-binding protein, providing valuable insights into its binding mechanisms and the importance of flexible DNA characteristics in protein-DNA interactions.

The universal entropy compression scheme developed by Alon, Naor, and Schuster-Thiele, has a theoretical limit to its optimal efficiency, which is hampered by non-constant overhead. We address this limitation by modifying the scheme to achieve polynomial-time complexity with minimal, constant-level losses in its optimal efficiency. Our experiments demonstrate that the improved scheme significantly outperforms conventional universal compression methods on synthetic data, with its maximum overhead being no more than half a byte. Furthermore, our implementation of this scheme on real-world text datasets has shown it to be faster and more space-efficient than the popular zstd algorithm.

Understanding how dielectric characteristics of pore fluid in cement-based materials change is essential for developing a reliable, non-invasive method to analyze these materials over a long period of time. In a recent study, we examined how temperature, water content, and the presence of calcium ions affect the dielectric properties of these materials' pore fluids within frequencies between 1 and 30 MHz. Our results revealed that dielectric constants and loss tangents of the pore fluids are significantly influenced by temperature and the concentration of calcium ions, but not by the water content, within the studied ranges. Our findings can help expand the application of non-invasive monitoring methods for cement-based materials and improve their performance.

In the context of Quantum Chromodynamics, we explore the heavy-heavy hadronic clusters, including their quark compositions and the potential model for their binding. We also investigate the mass and decay widths of these clusters, and compare our findings with the existing D0 and Bc meson data. Our results indicate that the charmonium state is the most lightest among the charmed hadronic clusters. Additionally, we discuss the potential implications of the spectral series of heavy-heavy hadronic clusters for the quark-model predictions and the compact quark configuration.

This study investigates the advancements in military swarms of unmanned drones through an examination of publicly available information such as news articles, press releases, and industry reports. By applying natural language processing techniques, the research aims to gain insights into the driving factors behind these technological improvements. A substantial body of literature has been created using natural language models to facilitate this analysis.

The correlations of a three-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ forest signal, specifically its slope, amplitude, and curvature, are shown to be strongly linked to fundamental parameters, like baryon density, matter density, and amplitude, which can be precisely determined from three-year data collected by the SDSS-III. By cross-correlating Lyman-$\alpha$ galaxies with SDSS-II galaxy samples, researchers were able to eliminate potential foreground contamination and isolate the impact of line correlations on cosmological models, yielding a unique and unbiased result. Furthermore, the study reveals how varying the Eisenstein parameter, $\beta$, affects the slope and curvature of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest correlations, ultimately allowing for tighter constraints on cosmological models and shedding new light on issues such as Hubble tension and early universe power spectrum properties.

In this study, researchers have demonstrated a new emittance transfer technique, employing a specially designed beam-shaping filter to transfer emittance from a limiting slit aperture to a limiting radio-frequency (RF) cavity. A carefully crafted tungsten filter has been used to shift the emittance-limiting slits in the x, y planes and the cx, cy axes to the emittance-limiting RF cavity. As a result, researchers have achieved a significant reduction in emittance, demonstrating a 10% shrinkage in both horizontal and longitudinal emittances at the LCLS. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications for beam transport, enabling a more precise matching of beam parameters and minimizing the impact of RF cavities on beam quality.

Recent studies have shown that using a single global context in trajectory forecasting can lead to significant performance losses. This concept paper proposes a novel approach to jointly forecast multiple trajectories by considering local and social contexts dynamically. The proposed method involves sliding a Rethinking module over a sequence of multiple trajectory frames, allowing it to adapt to varying social contexts and determine which components to use at each step. This enables the Rethinking module to improve performance and provide a better understanding of pedestrian behavior. Experimental results on the ETH and UCF dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

A novel approach to quantifying the complexity of Boltzmann machines is presented, incorporating two information theory-based measures, mutual information and entropy rates, which respectively gauge internal consistency and external randomness in the models. Through numerical experiments conducted on Boltzmann learning automata, the efficacy of these metrics is evaluated and demonstrated to be particularly useful in distinguishing between different environmental dynamics and revealing a specific form of organization in the models. These findings suggest that the chosen measures are sensitive to distinct aspects of the models, with mutual information gauging organization and entropy rates detecting disorder, and that their combined use can effectively capture the organization and dynamics of the models.

The increased presence of drones in daily life has led to a growing need for reliable swarm-human interaction techniques that enable intuitive control of drones through motion-based commands. This study focuses on developing a sophisticated hand motion recognition system to efficiently manage swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles remotely. The system incorporates a cutting-edge hand keypoint detection technology, leveraging pose estimation powered by a machine learning model, to accurately track hand movements. The system's capabilities are demonstrated through actual field experiments, showcasing its effectiveness in correctly identifying hand gestures and successfully utilizing these motions to perform drone-related tasks.

The study examines the efficacy of combining neural network models with voting mechanisms for blood cell classification. By analyzing a 256-channel blood cell image dataset, the research evaluates various neural architecture search methods, including Unstructured NAS-BenchCell and Structured NAS-BenchCell, as well examines combining strategies such as sum, mean, vote, and attention-based combinations. The unstructured search achieved an accuracy of 97.7%, while the structured search resulted in an accuracy of 98.0%. The unstructured NAS-BenchCell model demonstrated the best performance when employing a vote-based strategy, reaching 98.1% accuracy. The remaining author affiliations are listed in Appendix~\ref{sec:app:author_affiliation}.

A widely used method in quantum many-body physics for studying ground-state properties is the Hubbard model. Developing efficient methods to create ground-state-like entanglement in this model is crucial. A novel approach, called the variational counterdiabatic (VCD) strategy, is introduced to create a time-dependent circuit that mimics the desired ground-state evolution. The VCDB strategy is tested on the one- and two-dimensional Hubbard models and demonstrates excellent performance by creating high fidelity with the target many-body state and reducing the computational complexity. A key advantage of VCDB is its ability to create entanglement without the excessive cost associated with existing methods, making it a valuable tool in quantum simulation and quantum computing.

A historical method for decolorizing images, known as decolorization, is explored in this paper, which examines its underlying principles through experimentation and research. New findings challenge and expand upon the traditional understanding of this technique's color transformation properties. Decolorization's adaptability and efficiency, coupled with its minimal computational requirements, make it a valuable tool for applications such as image decolorization, color-based security, color-based steganography, color-based data compression, color-based encryption, color-based fusion, and color correction. Our study presents a color difference formula under decolorization that is valid across all color temperatures and highlights its unique characteristic of maintaining positive correlation with luminance. Furthermore, a novel decolorization approach is developed that is valid across all color temperatures and highlights its distinctive features of high-velocity operation and hue preservation. Our findings suggest that this approach can be used for color-based applications that demand high-velocity processing and hue preservation.

We propose an advanced technique for accelerating matrix-based iterative algorithms used to approximate the matrix power series expansion of a composite function, specifically of the form $f(e^{A\Delta t})\mathbf{x}$. This technique efficiently computes the truncated exponential Taylor expansion of a matrix function by introducing an optimized evaluation algorithm that significantly reduces computational complexity compared to the naive approach, from $\mathcal{O}(N^3\log N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$. Furthermore, we've developed an error estimation method that enables determination of the necessary expansion order to achieve a prescribed relative error, thereby facilitating the adaptation of the expansion order to the eigenvalue spectrum of the matrix. The remaining challenge is to determine the optimal value of the shift parameter, which significantly enhances convergence, by minimizing the expansion polynomial's degree while maintaining accuracy.

Given a CAT($k$) surface with an outer boundary composed of at least two arcs, we demonstrate the existence of a continuous map from the upper half plane to this surface that meets three criteria: it uniformly converges to a harmonic function inside, its derivative is square-integrable, and its length is minimized. We further investigate the properties of these "harmonically branched" extensions, showing they extend to a closed upper half plane under certain circumstances, with implications for understanding Riemannian metrics on the boundary. Notably, if the surface has a non-zero total curvature, these extensions map to non-trivial functions, and we demonstrate that such extensions can be reparameterized as conformal maps to a new CAT($k$) surface, with the boundary becoming a simple closed curve. This result is applied to prove that any CAT($k$) surface with an outer boundary consisting of at least two arcs can be uniformly reparameterized such that at least one boundary arc becomes a line segment.

The intersection of laser-plasma and photon physics holds immense promise for developing novel light sources and conducting fundamental research in the field. Laser plasmas can generate high-energy photon ensembles through electron scattering and nonlinear processes, with the resulting photons capable of interacting with each other at sub-threshold energies, either directly or via virtual states. This review presents a comprehensive model that integrates laser-plasma and photon physics, focusing on the generation of X-ray and gamma-ray photons via electron scattering and the subsequent photon-photon interactions. A step-by-step framework is proposed, outlining the relative significance of various photon generation mechanisms and interaction processes, with the ultimate goal of identifying the most effective pathways for achieving specific scientific objectives.

This research examines the theoretical and experimental adaptability of the two Higgs doublet model (2HDM, type-1) to the off-diagonal, $CP$-violating parameter $A_{6i}$ in $B \to \pi \pi$ decays, a crucial aspect of $Z_2$ soft-breaking. The study focuses on the direct impact of $A_{6i}$ and its interplay with the Higgs-to-gluon coupling modifier, $\kappa_g$, a consequence of the new scalar boson, $H$, in the 2HDM. The research considers the 2HDM as an extension of the Standard Model (SM) and investigates how the 2HDM and $\kappa_g$ can be constrained by the ALICE and future Pbc experiments at the LHC, particularly in $B \to \pi \pi$ decay observables and Higgs searches in gluon-fusion channels. The findings of this research indicate that $A_{12} \lesssim 10^{-3}$ GeV$^2$ and $\kappa_g$ can be constrained to the range of $[0.95, 1.15]$ at a 95% confidence level, a significant step towards understanding the 2HDM and its off-diagonal, $CP$-violating parameter.

The effectiveness of data exchange in relational and graph data formats heavily relies on the compatibility of the conversion processes. The use of type annotations in relational schemas and graph shape expressions can enhance the reliability of data transformation processes. This study examines the impact of formal shape expressions on the translation of relational schemas into RDF graphs, focusing on the RDF-star extension that allows for the representation of first-order facts. By building on the existing knowledge of data exchange properties, the paper provides solutions for relational schema-transformation to RDF graphs under both RDF-star and traditional representation, ensuring compliance with the specified properties through shape expressions.

To effectively analyze data with parameters influenced by other variables, we require a boundary estimation method for a class of non-parametric functions. We propose a convex regression estimator that can be efficiently computed using a new Python library called pyStoNED. This library builds upon recent research on asymptotic properties of this estimator, allowing it to be freely available for both statistical applications and boundary-based derivative estimation. We demonstrate pyStoNED's versatility by applying it to three distinct problems: testing for mean-reversion, estimating VaR, and analyzing demand curves.

This study examines potential observable signals for a 125 GeV Higgs boson in four-lepton and two-lepton plus two-jet configurations produced via top quark pairs and additional bosons (Higgs or Z boson) at the Large Hadron Collider. The investigation is based on simulated data representing 300 inverse femtobarns of data collected with 14 TeV protons. The observed signals are compared to background signals from non-Higgs creation, which are reduced using a simple cut-based method. The observed signals for the creation of a 125 GeV Higgs boson via a W boson show a 2.4 sigma excess, while those from a Z boson creation show a 3.8 sigma excess. The observed signals significantly exceed those expected from standard model processes, indicating potential new physics.

We examine the capabilities and pitfalls of fully unsupervised and few-shot learning derived from large, pre-trained language models. Our research, conducted on natural datasets without domain-specific pre-training, reveals that models can sometimes learn meaningful representations, yet falter when tasked with few-shot learning. Additionally, we discover that model performance relies heavily on the training dataset's distribution, with certain datasets yielding superior results. Our study also demonstrates that model effectiveness improves significantly when using task-specific pre-training on a diverse range of datasets, and we demonstrate that dataset fine-tuning can enhance model results without incurring substantial computational costs.

This project aims to create a platform for utilizing automated speech recognition services.
Currently, speech models are predominantly commercial and support a limited range of languages.
In contrast, open-source speech systems are available at no cost, but are typically underserved by data and lack support for smaller languages.
Nonetheless, German speech models based on a substantial dataset have been successfully developed.
These models are trained using Tensorflow and can be efficiently fine-tuned for various applications.
The project aims to make these speech models accessible for both end-users and developers.
By automating the process of integrating the speech model, a complete solution is offered that includes a web interface and an open REST API.
The REST API can be easily integrated with other software, and the web interface provides a user-friendly platform for speech-to-text conversion.
The project consists of a web service that accepts audio input and returns text, a user-friendly interface for speech recognition, and a comprehensive documentation of the speech model and its usage.

The 30 Doradus nebula, part of the Large Magellanic Cloud, is the most luminous star cluster within this galaxy, making it a valuable object for studying the properties of star populations. Characterizing the Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus nebula, which are defined by their excess emission in spectral lines due to gaseous disks, is crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of these stars. In this study, we examine the properties of Be-type stars in 30 Doradus, which we identified using Gaia data, by analyzing their spectral characteristics, rotation rates, and spectral type distributions. We found that the Be-type stars in 30 Doradus have moderate rotation rates, with most having rotational periods less than their critical rotation, and that the distribution of spectral types is consistent with theoretical models of these stars.

Contrary to the typical data enhancement practice of creating more content from less, our study uses a method to refine content by combining two entries with similar meanings. This technique was applied in a medical context to standardize complex drug names, also known as textual EIDs, by integrating them with corresponding structured data from medical event codes, similar to SNOMED CT or ATC. The conventional approach involves combining textual EIDs and their corresponding structured representations into a single representation learning task, but this method has a significant limitation due to the scarcity of aligned pairs. To overcome this challenge, we developed two data augmentation methods that generate an optimized training dataset, allowing the model to learn the connection between the two modalities more effectively. The experimental results confirm the efficacy of the proposed methods, demonstrating their ability to enhance data-driven inverse text standardization.

This research investigates the Faber-Krahn inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Galeron-Morlet operator, subject to the Robin boundary condition. We demonstrate that the ball constitutes a minimal configuration, and derive a precise asymptotic expansion of the first eigenvalue. This achievement relies on utilizing the symmetrization technique pioneered by Hardy, Littlewood, and Polya, in conjunction with specific estimates for the Hermite polynomials.

The increasing interest in online learning has led to the development of tangent kernel theory, which enables the learning of data exchangeable under rotations. However, not all tasks involving data exchangeable data follow a rotational rotation, and some data that is exchangeable can also be learned with traditional methods that treat data as independently and identically distributed. This study proposes the exploration of other data exchangeability groups and their associated kernels. A new framework is introduced, which allows for the definition of novel kernels for tasks other than rotational learning and groups other than rotations. Specifically, a non-orthogonal transformation kernel is defined, which can learn data exchangeable under a wider range of linear transformations. Additionally, a non-identifiable tangent kernel is defined to handle situations where the transformation matrix cannot be identified. These findings are supported by theoretical results and empirical evidence.

The point gap in the spectrum of non-Hermitian systems holds pivotal significance in the study of topological phases. In this research, we establish a criterion for the presence of non-trivial point gap topology in non-Hermitian systems by employing the concept of winding numbers in a modified non-Hermitian index theorem. The derivation of this criterion necessitates the consideration of both the non-Hermitian and standard gap conditions, and it is demonstrated that, in certain scenarios, these requirements can be superseded by the emergence of complex conjugate pairs. Furthermore, we illustrate the efficacy of the proposed criterion through the analysis of non-Hermitian systems with and without long-range correlations, and it is shown that, while correlations can induce a phase transition, they can also result in a partial or complete elimination of the point gap topology.

A speaker's social characteristics, such as their social status or social class, can be identified through their voice and are integral to the concept of social speaker attributes. These attributes play a crucial role in conversations, as they convey information about the speaker's personality and social background. To address the need for more realistic and socially nuanced synthetic speech, we examine how these social characteristics affect the parameters of a phonetic model and explore the methods for incorporating them into the synthesis process.

A well-known, modular A4 model that incorporates discrete flavor symmetries, has been successfully applied to describe both fermion masses and neutrino oscillation phenomena at observable energy levels. Meanwhile, dark matter remains unaccounted for. To address this deficit, we've developed a novel, A4-invariant dark matter framework incorporating a U(1) B-L symmetry, where a complex representation of the A4 group in the fermion sector and the luminosity of dark matter annihilation are naturally generated. Moreover, the model's naturalness and testability at the LHC are also explored.

Building on the concept of deformation in nuclei, we introduce a novel approach inspired by the uncertainty principle, where the Deformed Minimal Length Uncertainty Principle is applied to the Interacting Boson Model of triaxial nuclei. A novel mathematical framework has been developed, allowing for a more precise description of nuclear behavior. Results of this approach align closely with experimental data, particularly in terms of energy levels and transition probabilities, for nuclei such as $^{124}$Sn and $^{152}$Gd. Furthermore, we examine how the minimal length parameter affects the dynamics of nuclear systems.

This paper presents novel methods for creating golay codes and complementary sets, including complex and real golay codes, and a new method to generate real golay codes from real symmetric matrices of a specific type. It also provides a matrix-based method for creating Cremona sets, including a general method to create golay codes and a method to create a specific type of matrix from any matrix of a certain dimension. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates a method to create Cremona sets from matrix pairs, including a way to create golay codes from matrix pairs and a method to create a pair of matrices from a cremona set pair.

In this research, we introduce a novel, efficient approach utilizing artificial intelligence to identify alterations in complex images. The proposed method employs a novel architecture, known as Feature Combination Deep Convolutional Autoencoders (FC-CDAE), which efficiently processes detailed, multi-dimensional data by integrating multiple processing layers. FC-CDAE encodes the differential information between two images, and subsequently encodes the combined encoded features. The reconstruction of these images is then analyzed using a statistical model to detect alterations. The proposed approach is evaluated on three hyperspectral image datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately identifying alterations. Notably, the proposed method outperforms existing techniques, with an average accuracy improvement of 11.4% in dataset A, 12.2% in dataset B, and 13.4% in dataset C.

A computer simulation study examined how viscosity in a variety of molecular fluids is connected to residual entropy, utilizing data from experiments and simulations. Our investigation revealed that a particular thermodynamic relationship holds true for a wide range of molecular fluids when a specific type of interaction is present. Additionally, we proposed an improved formula for viscosity that takes into account the residual entropy, specifically tailored for molecules with typical covalent bonds. Furthermore, we investigated how the orientation-dependent part of the interaction influences viscosity, revealing that its effect is more significant than previously thought. Our findings shed new light on the characteristics of molecular fluids and molecular interactions, contributing to existing theories.

The $Lambda CDM$ cosmological model, despite its success, faces significant drawbacks due to an unreasonably large $Lambda$ value and excessive entropy in the universe. A novel, self-correcting cyclical model, incorporating these factors, resolves these issues by eliminating the necessity for $Lambda$ after the baryon epoch, substituting it with dark energy that triggers a universe expansion leading to a rapid contraction and subsequent rebirth of the cosmos. This model, characterized by its internal balance, presents a self-sustaining cycle of matter creation and destruction.

The Invariant-set hypothesis, first introduced in the 1990s, posits a hidden-variable value pair's location within a specific geometric structure that replicates quantum probabilities. This concept, categorized as a superdeterministic, local hidden-variable theory, claims to resolve the dilemma posed by the Bell inequality. We demonstrate that this hypothesis is a more general form of superdeterminism, thereby enabling it to account for the Bell inequality's results, provided the model adheres to non-local constraints. We identify three key assumptions underpinning the hypothesis, and highlight that one is particularly significant, namely the concept that hidden-variable values are confined to a 2D plane. This, combined with the model's non-local nature, implies the possibility of constructing the desired probability distribution through local means, and suggests potential avenues for generating this distribution using simple non-local, superdeterministic models.

Incorporating neural networks in IoT devices necessitates careful consideration of their implementation, particularly when it comes to keyphrase detection. These models, typically hosted in the cloud due to limited local resources, require an initial step of extracting keyphrases from raw text on the device. Directly utilizing full datasets, such as 100,000-word Python code change logs, would be inefficient in terms of memory usage and power consumption. As a result, we devised a novel system consisting of two machine learning models, a shallow neural network-based keyphrase detector and a shallow neural network-based keyphrase reducer, both designed to operate effectively on embedded IoT devices. We evaluated the performance of these models using a dataset of 250,000 Python change logs and found that the system significantly reduces the number of key phrases from 60 to 10, while also demonstrating better accuracy in fault prediction. Furthermore, the keyphrase reduction rate is positively correlated with prediction accuracy, with an average reduction rate of 80%.

The critical behavior of nonchiral fermings on a two-dimensional lattice is analyzed in conjunction with dimers, where an external gauge field influences both fields. A prior study on the statistical mechanics of dimers established a connection between this framework and fermionic theories. Building on this foundation, we investigate the effects of this gauge field on the lattice fermings. Employing an exact mapping method and a field-theoretic approach, we demonstrate that this nonchiral ferm system exhibits a form of self-screening that compensates for the gauge field's influence. As a result, the dimers-fermion correspondence holds true for all values of the gauge field. Furthermore, when the number of dimers becomes large, we derive an explicit formula for the free energy and verify a form of Fermi-liquid behavior. Our findings also extend to the case of the chiral dimer model, where we establish a connection to massless Dirac sea in the presence of a background gauge field, where the dimers susceptibility mimics the magnetic moment of the Dirac sea under large gauge fields.

The Group Lasso method, an extension of the Lasso for grouped variable selection, has several modified versions for handling data of different types. Three of these modifications are presented, along with an analysis of their performance and convergence. To evaluate their practical effectiveness, both theoretical proofs and simulation experiments demonstrate the method's capabilities, which further enable the development of a tailored approach for analyzing high-dimensional nominal data using the method.

System reliability is a major concern for embedded real-time systems, particularly those found in safety-critical applications like autonomous vehicles and industrial robots. To address this challenge, a concept called Importance-Based Isolation has been proposed, which segregates processes based on their priority and level of importance to enhance the systems overall reliability. Previous efforts have explored this approach through a combination of virtualization technology and real-time scheduling methods, but these approaches have often been constrained by their reliance on non-deterministic virtualization technologies, which can introduce unpredictable behavior and limit performance. To overcome these limitations, we have developed T-Visor, a novel hypothesis designed to efficiently manage processes of varying importance in real-time environments. Leveraging the TimeVex architecture, T-Visor minimizes both the overhead and latency variability caused by a hypervisor, thereby ensuring precise scheduling of user processes and the ability to support multiple scheduling policies. We have also incorporated automated mechanisms to facilitate the isolation of processes with different importance levels, enabling the system to adapt to different operational scenarios. Through a series of experiments, we have demonstrated the practicality and effectiveness of T-Visor in a variety of scenarios, including a comparison with existing software-based solutions and an evaluation of its performance in comparison to the actual operating systems used in applications similar to autonomous vehicles and robotic systems.

Panoramic stitching from multiple high-resolution images is a complex and time-consuming process due to the need for accurate camera parameters, especially when dealing with simple features that are not sufficient for guiding the stitching process. Existing methods utilizing feature points often struggle with precise camera positioning, and deep learning-based solutions are limited by their reliance on specific architectures and the need for significant computational resources. This paper presents an innovative approach that leverages the principles of gravity to determine the orientation of cameras, thereby providing precise camera parameters with minimal camera movements. By assuming that images are captured in a consistent direction, the proposed method can be trained on a diverse range of camera models and achieve high-precision camera positioning even with simple image features. Furthermore, the proposed technique enables efficient camera pose optimization and stitching for high-resolution images, resulting in superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce a concept of dispersion heterogeneity in networks, leading to distinct heterogeneous regions with clear boundaries but distinct internal connections. Chimeras with dispersed heterogeneity emerge in networks of coupled oscillators, characterized by coexisting synchronized and asynchronous groups within each heterogeneously distributed sub-network. Bifurcation analysis reveals the existence of stable and unstable standing waves in two-group networks with end-to-end and ring topologies, where standing waves feature phases with identical gradients, resulting in S-shaped curves of the real eigenvalue for loss of stability.

In this research, we focus on developing controllers for systems that can withstand unexpected disturbances, focusing on a critical category of problems - those where controllers can't be explicitly designed due to the vast number of possible scenarios. We propose an innovative approach called a probabilistic model for situation transition, which enables us to find the best course of action in each scenario to achieve our desired outcome with the least amount of disruption. By leveraging this concept, we introduce a new method called a Probabilistic Model-Driven Policy Search, which learns situation-dependent controllers that can adapt to and minimize system disruption. Our proposed algorithm was put to the test on linear systems and demonstrated its ability to outperform other methods, ultimately reducing cost.

A multi-layer diagram is defined as an infinite collection of elements sourced from a collection of graded modules over the polynomial ring in two variables, with increasingly high degrees of elements as the size of the set grows. The concept is then related to the slice rings of the form R/(f1,...,fs), where R is a two-variable polynomial ring and fi are homogeneous polynomials, with a focus on a specific class of slice rings termed as stable. The text also examines the connection between these stable rings and multi-layer diagrams and presents examples of both finite and infinite multi-layer diagrams.

We introduce the concept of refracted entropy, an extension of refracted entropy in holographic theories, for use within generic quantum systems and tensor networks. Within the context of holography, our definition aligns perfectly with its gravitational counterpart, resulting in identical numerical outcomes. Our research focuses primarily on chaotic unitary dynamics within random tensor networks, a fundamental model for understanding entanglement dynamics in quantum systems and gravitational systems alike. Within this framework, we observe that refracted entropy accurately captures the phase transitions of refracted entropy, exhibiting distinct behavior across these regimes. Notably, its behavior varies significantly across these phases, ranging from linear growth and saturation to complex oscillatory patterns.

We introduce a general approach for extracting inheritable information from stochastic systems across various scales, capable of retaining this information in the most unpredictable environments and transferring it between systems regardless of their complexity. This method is an extension of Renyi's channel capacity but has a crucial distinction: it quantifies information that can be passed from one generation to another, even in the most chaotic scenarios, and can be applied to channels of any statistical nature, including those defined by random variables, probability distributions, and other unpredictable systems, all of which reduce to the same underlying pattern of information transfer that can be passed down through generations. This method is calculated using the maximum mutual information between the most similar patterns in the input and output channels, and we provide a comprehensive explanation of this concept, its theoretical foundation, and its practical applications, including its use in analyzing gene expression patterns, brain activity, and other complex systems.

We introduce an algorithm to generate and display the invariant set resulting from the pullback of the three-dimensional generalized H\'{e}non map with a large mapping parameter. By employing a basic computer, the algorithm produces a three-dimensional graphic that illustrates the intricate fractal shape of this invariant set, showcasing self-similar patterns on a minute scale. Furthermore, we examine how altering a single map parameter influences the invariant set and discuss the inherent instability of this set.

We demonstrate that the holonomy of the connection associated with the metric, as defined by the Drinfel'd double structure group, under the condition of being versioned, converges to a unique expression in the limit of the large metric, thereby revealing the definitive form of the holonomy. This can be seen to correspond to the phase holonomy in the context of the Connes-Lott noncommutative geometry. Furthermore, by establishing a correspondence between the holonomy and the noncommutative star product, we show that this phase holonomy can also be derived from the noncommutative geometry framework when employing the large metric limit.

We are examining specific distributions of certain types of partitions into smaller groups, particularly those in which the size of each individual hook length is divisible by either 2 or 3. Our analysis focuses on proving that certain combinatorial sequences are accurate, providing further insight into generalized counting principles. Additionally, our findings include the establishment of a principle and the identification of an intriguing pattern in another sequence, offering a partial explanation for an unproven conjecture.

The concept of tunneling duration has long been a subject of debate, with no consensus reached. A widely accepted mathematical expression for tunneling time is $\tau = \hbar \Delta k / \Gamma$, where $\Delta k$ represents the momentum width and $\Gamma$ is the decay width. This paper challenges the validity of this accepted expression by comparing it to the Larmor clock method, a reliable timing technique for tunneling particles. Using the Larmor clock to measure a particle's tunneling time when it enters the tunneling barrier in a spin-up state yields a result of $\tau = \hbar (2\Delta k)^2 / \Gamma$, which differs significantly from the commonly accepted expression. The new formula for tunneling time is then validated using two different models: a spin-orbit coupled square barrier and a circular barrier.

This research explores the internal structure of heavy P-wave mesons. We utilize the light-cone QCD sum rules to analyze how the distribution of the dominant twist distribution of the heavy P-wave mesons changes with the momentum fraction x. The findings reveal that, in P-wave mesons, the dominant twist distribution distribution is skewed towards extreme values of x or (1-x). Furthermore, our results suggest that the P-wave charmonium and bottomonium dominant twist distribution profiles exhibit a similar shape but differ in the magnitude of the central dip, with the P-wave charmonium dip being deeper than its P-wave bottomonium counterpart.

We analyze the behavior of quantum switches based on Bose-Einstein condensates and control their characteristics with a specific potential, and our results indicate that the switching capabilities can be adjusted by changing the system's parameters in order to accommodate various applications.

We provide a detailed study of the double soft limit of n-gluon amplitudes, focusing on the role of the BMS algebra at null infinity. Using the chiral representation of the celestial holographicity program, we derive the central extension of the BMS algebra that arises in this limit.

In the real world, situations often arise where a model is unable to accurately predict certain data points, which typically results in a pre-trained model being underperforming.  This 'ageing' issue is particularly challenging for time-sensitive applications.  This paper proposes an innovative approach to address the 'ageing' issue in continual learning scenarios.  Our novel neural architecture, designed for learning structures within graphs, enables real-time learning and is capable of identifying regions within the feature space where the model is failing, which in turn enables a more effective model to be selected.  Our approach also enables the seamless integration of newly acquired knowledge into the existing model, effectively mitigating the 'ageing' issue.  Our experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR10, and Caltech10, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, which significantly outperforms traditional neural network baselines, achieving state-of-the-art results, with accuracy levels as high as 99.5% and 97.2% respectively, while maintaining select model performance.

We define and analyze the properties of the formal Riemannian tensor $E$, which represents a standard form for a four-dimensional metric. Our investigation into this formal structure reveals it to be a symplectic form with its associated Legendre structure, enabling us to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for $E$ to satisfy certain algebraic symmetries and a simplified algebraic condition. Furthermore, we find that $E$ can be expressed as a Hamiltonian form, which also corresponds to a cosymplectic form, and explore its implications for the construction of a global structure. In the context of four-dimensions, we discover that $E$ decomposes into a combination of two measures and investigate their interrelations and properties. Our research also establishes a connection between $E$ and a Hamiltonian function $H$, and explore the implications of $H$ being Casimir. Our findings show that the four-dimensional metric is Ricci-flat if and only if $H$ satisfies a specific condition, and we provide an alternative expression for $H$ based on the associated symplectic measure.

We examine permutation functions and complete functions over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ where $q$ is a prime power, and further explore suitable functions in this context for cryptographic purposes.

This research proposes an efficient method for categorizing deep belief networks into specific groups based on their worm characteristics, which can aid in creating tailored treatments. The occurrence of worm infections is particularly high in developing nations, where limited resources often result in the use of a single treatment for all types of worms. To address this issue, the study introduces a novel technique for automatically categorizing six worm types using only raw intestinal images, which trains a deep belief network to accurately identify the types of worms present.

This research introduces a type of non-zero-sum game involving two players, the investment and reinsurance strategies of whom are influenced by a regime-switching jump-diffusion model. An objective function is designed to measure each player's risk and performance, and a dynamic programming method is used to prove the existence of an equilibrium for the model. However, due to the complexity of solving nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations numerically, a machine learning approach based on deep neural networks is used to approximate the optimal strategies and value functions, thereby allowing for the estimation of the strategies under varying parameters. Finally, numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method.

This study develops a novel flight control method using adjustable wing devices controlled by rotors, designed to handle fluid instabilities. The algorithm combines a dual simplex method with a finite element mesh coarsening technique to achieve a stable and efficient rotor control. The results demonstrate the model's ability to maintain steady flight and adaptively learn optimal rotor settings to mitigate oscillations and install vortex effects.

The characterization of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy levels is crucial,
with the S-wave scattering length being the defining factor. The Goldstone theorem dictates that this length must be inverse-proportional to the pion mass, necessitating the inclusion of the pion's dynamical role within the sigma model. This ensures the necessary non-linear derivative couplings and self-interactions of pions, which are essential for accurately representing pion-nucleon interactions. The parameters for these interactions are self-adjustable within the sigma model, thanks to the dynamical role of pions, which necessitates chiral symmetry breaking. Consequently, only one parameter, the pion decay constant, remains essential for accurately representing low-energy pion-nucleon interactions. This self-adjustability and the dominance of the self-interaction term over the pion-nucleon coupling are key in achieving local chiral symmetry breaking and self-consistently representing pion-nucleon interactions.

High-energy particle collisions in the Large Hadron Collider generate complex dense tracks, making them difficult to reconstruct, especially across boundary regions between detector segments. This challenge is particularly pronounced at the edge of endcap pixel detectors due to significant tilt angles. We introduce a novel algorithm, leveraging the iterative correction of hits to translate between local and global coordinate systems, showing improved performance in simulating DEPFOS technology and degrading minimally with real data from the CMS pixel detector, while outperforming existing reconstruction methods.

We have developed an efficient method for classifying galaxies by shape using image data. This approach leverages an image classifier trained on artificially created galaxy shapes, allowing for shape classification of galaxies in the z<1 range. By combining this shape classification with redshift data from spectroscopy, we can directly associate AGN with their host galaxies and identify any misclassified shapes. Our study utilized approximately 1000 spectroscopic samples from the z<1 range, classifying them into early-type galaxies, late-type galaxies, and buffer galaxies. Early- and late-type galaxies were based on shape, with buffer galaxies serving as a control group. We then trained a shape classifier on HSC images of approximately 100,000 galaxies, achieving a classification accuracy of 80% for galaxies with signal-to-noise ratios greater than 10. Applying this shape classifier to the HSC Wide Survey yielded 14,000 galaxies, allowing us to compare their shapes with those in the z<1 sample and identify any shape biases.

At low-momentum, atoms exhibit a heightened likelihood of correlation, known as short-range correlations. This study delves into the SRCS phenomenon, creating a framework for generating and visualizing probability distributions of particles correlated within a specified sphere in momentum space. To achieve this, the authors have devised a universal method, enabling a comprehensive understanding of the SRCS phenomenon through four distinct phase-space probability distributions. This work is focused on SRCS in the context of light nuclei, but the developed approach is universally applicable to any systems exhibiting short-range correlations.

Deep learning systems rely heavily on floating-point precision, which is essential for both training accuracy and performance. The commonly used equality check in deep learning frameworks fails to account for this precision, often leading to incorrect behavior. As complex numbers are crucial in certain deep learning applications, such as multivariate time series analysis, our proposed co-domain equality充分考虑了 the co-domain of functions and is applicable to both real and complex domains. The experiments demonstrate that incorporating co-domain equality yields better model accuracy and performance, while also reducing memory consumption and data transfer time.

The non-linear Saturated Gluon Field, influenced by the saturation scale $Q_s$, exhibits geometric scaling where cross sections depend on the variable $\ln(xQ_s^2/\Lambda^2)$. This characteristic is evident in various observables such as total cross sections, Reggeon exchange processes, and certain kinematic regimes of vector meson production in Deep Inelastic ep scattering. Furthermore, similar behavior is seen in vector meson production in pA and AA collisions, as well as high-energy nuclear collisions exhibiting a saturation disk signature across multiple energy ranges, all of which are in line with experimental data.

The vast diversity of chemical compositions among low-metallicity stars in the Milky Way's halo and the satellite galaxy, the Magellanic Clouds, is thought to be a reflection of the chemical compositions of the early galaxy. This diversity challenges our understanding of the chemical evolution of these systems. To explore the origins of this abundance spread, we conducted a comprehensive study of chemical data from 11 low-metallicity systems, including 145 carbon stars and 145 S-type giants, by examining their carbon and s-process element abundances. Our study reveals a notable negative correlation between nitrogen and barium abundances, suggesting a relationship between nitrogen and s-process element abundances. This, in turn, indicates that rapid neutron capture processes are less affected by nitrogen abundances, and that abundance spread is likely due to the varying rates of rapid neutron capture in early supernovae.

This study introduces a comprehensive toolkit, known as Sensitivity Explorer (SEx), designed to assess the performance of various machine learning models across different levels of in-sample sensitivity and out-of-sample generalization. The SEx toolkit enables users to identify the optimal machine learning model for a given problem, taking into account different levels of in-sample sensitivity and out-of-sample generalization based on a single, unified hyperparameter. By doing so, it streamlines the model selection process and eliminates the need for complex search procedures. The toolkit is illustrated through its application to financial literacy forecasting, where replicating and matching the performance of a linear benchmark is made effortless. Additionally, the tool allows for the evaluation of multiple models under varying levels of in-sample sensitivity and even identifies scenarios where linear regression remains the superior choice.

This study introduces a SQUID-based approach to teach classical neural networks interactively with quantum phenomena. We examined SQUID's effectiveness in training two types of neural networks, binary and MNIST, and found that the SQUID method was more efficient, particularly when there are limited data points available. Furthermore, the research highlights the potential for educators to incorporate quantum computing principles into learning by utilizing SQUID technology, opening up new possibilities for exploring quantum computing and facilitating learning.

Two novel distorted product structures have been proposed in this research, leading to
the definition of a distorted product scheme for submanifolds. We then examine
the distorted product scheme of nearly conformal contact submanifolds, leading to
the introduction of a new near conformal contact distorted product scheme. We
specifically study nearly conformal contact Hamiltonian distorted product scheme
submanifolds and distorted conformal symplectic Hamiltonian distorted product
scheme submanifolds, and investigate their key characteristics. Additionally, we
define and investigate certain distorted product points of nearly conformal contact
Hamiltonian and nearly conformal contact symplectic submanifolds, and provide
two examples to illustrate these concepts.

A rising interest in inactive nuclear recoil examination arises from advancements in multiple areas of nuclear physics, including low-energy nuclear reactions, in situ low-energy neutron scattering, and nuclear recoil detection for dark matter research. Recently, defect-induced color centers in boron-doped diamond have emerged as a compelling tool for in situ detection applications due to their long lifetime and robust physical properties. This research paper introduces a new approach to in situ detection, known as PALEOCCEne, leveraging color centers in BDD to identify low-energy nuclear recoils. The proposed technique employs the readout of nitrogen-vacancy, diamond, and solid-state nuclear reaction spin states to detect recoil events resulting from superelastic neutron scattering, while also highlighting critical technical considerations and developing computational models to describe the underlying detection process.

We examine the movement of a particle within an area with varying levels of activity, where our study is based on solutions generated from a model that incorporates a particle influenced by a surrounding medium of smaller particles. By utilizing statistical methods and a mathematical approach, we develop a description of the particle's movement that takes into account both its position and speed. This results in coupled stochastic equations that simulate particle behavior in a wide range of scenarios, where the activity gradient affects particle movement and direction. However, this effect is constrained by specific conditions and may not be observed under certain conditions. Our study also highlights that the activity gradient can contribute to a particle's movement in a way that is comparable to thermal agitation, and may be significant in biological settings where molecules play a crucial role.

The fractional quantum Hall effect exhibits distinct and well-isolated excited states known as magnetorotons, which play a crucial role in understanding the dissipative properties of these systems. Traditionally, researchers assumed a single m=0 magnetoroton excited state existed for each fraction, but this view has been challenged by the discovery of multiple magneton states. In this study, we investigate a system of N electrons confined to a two-dimensional plane under a strong perpendicular magnetic field, applying the Haldane-Gap hypothesis and employing variational wave functions based on multiple magnetons and different angular momentum sectors. Our research reveals that states with varying numbers of magnetons exhibit different degrees of spectral regulation, characterized by a gap in their energy spectra. We find that while the singly-filled m=0 magneton state displays complete spectral regulation, states containing two m=0 magnetons or one m=1 magneton demonstrate incomplete regulation, exhibiting two spectral gaps. Furthermore, our results show that the spectral gaps in these states are significantly smaller than that of the singly-filled m=0 magneton state, with the first gap being approximately half the energy of the second gap.

Identifying and analyzing outbreaks on complex network structures is crucial for understanding and containing real-world epidemics, which often spread through structured populations such as social connections, geographical locations, or temporal interactions. Despite advancements in outbreak detection and analysis methods, limited research has been done on developing algorithms to identify clusters of connected outbreak nodes on networks, which is essential for creating and testing effective containment strategies. This study proposes a novel geometric approach to identify clusters of connected outbreak nodes on networks, demonstrating its effectiveness with theoretical performance guarantees and successful applications on real-world and synthetic datasets.

When creating maximum likelihood maps for the Cosmic Microwave Background, the assumption that a point source's time series follows a sinusoidal pattern can be compromised by this assumption. Researchers have previously attributed violations, known as 'X-es', to incorrect origin positioning in the time domain. This study revisits the problem of point source modeling and maps, exploring various methods for optimal map estimation and exhibiting the emergence of X-es. It then presents novel techniques to circumvent the application of sinusoidal patterns, thereby significantly reducing the occurrence of X-es, while demonstrating through simulated data the continued benefit of these methods in improving map quality.

We examine how goal-oriented reinforcement learning agents interpret verbal instructions. Specifically, we investigate how these agents prioritize verbal cues against their existing knowledge about available actions. We discovered that when multiple state conditions could potentially achieve a task, agents typically identify the easiest state change to make, instead of the most relevant one semantically. This problem, known as referential ambiguity, poses significant challenges for natural language-driven learning. We developed a statistical model to assess the likelihood of a condition being correctly referenced, and used it to test our findings. Our results demonstrate that in scenarios with numerous available actions, the effects of referential ambiguity become increasingly pronounced, ultimately hindering successful task completion. Furthermore, we propose two potential solutions: a language-enriched reward system and a form of action bias, which we demonstrate can effectively address this problem and promote robust task acquisition.

Quantum process tomography is a method used to determine an arbitrary quantum process. A proposed "shadow" approach for tomography is derived from quantum process shadow tomography, which is based on the Pauli measurement approach, utilizing randomly selected Pauli measurements. Furthermore, it is proven that the symmetric informationally complete (SIC) measurement provides an optimal method for minimizing the number of measurements required to achieve specific accuracy in quantum process tomography, demonstrating that SIC measurement reduces the required measurements by a factor of three compared to the random Pauli measurements method.

In this study, we establish specific regions for the Cheeger constant of two-dimensional shapes by deriving precise bounds in relation to fundamental geometric properties such as perimeter, area, inradius, and circumradius. Our investigation also includes detailed analysis of regular polygons and certain classes of two-dimensional shapes, including disks, ellipses, and triangles.

This study addresses a drone pathway design issue where flight routes must be
planned between designated points within a defined time frame. The research
investigates how limited battery life affects the solution approach and develops
an algorithm that takes into account the drone's battery capacity to ensure it
reaches its destination before it runs out of power. The paper also expands on
the initial model to accommodate multiple drones and different types of time
restrictions. To enhance computational efficiency, the authors created a new
method to generate symmetrical model representations, which significantly
reduces computation time when using a solvers. The paper concludes by testing
the proposed model on a range of instances, including those with numerous drones
and varying time restrictions, and evaluates the solution quality for instances
with limited power. The research builds upon a previous study by implementing
additional features to improve its applicability to real-world scenarios.

The critical behavior of interaction-relevant bilayer graphene is investigated using renormalization group analysis. Specifically, the irreversibility of Renormalization Group flow in the theoretical framework is demonstrated through explicit calculation of beta functions for relevant coupling constants in bilayer graphene models. As the value of the relevant coupling increases, it triggers a gradual transition from perturbative to non-perturbative renormalization group analysis, ultimately destabilizing both the bilayer and the theoretical framework itself. The instability in the bilayer is characterized by the emergence of a gap in the energy spectrum, whereas the theoretical instability is associated with the occurrence of fermion instability in the same context.
