This study examines the applications of lightweight cryptography on IoT devices characterized by low energy capabilities. As a key component of such devices, cryptographic components play a vital role in ensuring their data security and integrity. The document will discuss several forms of cryptography, including symmetric and asymmetric cryptography, hash functions, and MAC generation, as well as several lightweight variants. The introduction of this paper will cover the fundamental concepts of each of these categories, which will serve as a foundation for a deeper exploration of them in the context of IoT technology.

To determine precise physical constants, Ramsey spectroscopy serves as a foundational approach. However, the conventional Ramsey method is susceptible to measurement inaccuracies stemming from uncertainty in the free precession frequency's phase. This phase uncertainty leads to a bias in the estimated value, an issue that has been overlooked in many analyses. This paper introduces a novel trial-adjusting technique to mitigate this limitation, incorporating both the precision and accuracy of the estimated value into the adjustment process. This strategy benefits from the precision offered by a suitably adjusted adaptive sequencing of trial periods, while eliminating the bias associated with the standard approach. Furthermore, this method aligns with the Cramera-Rao lower bound and does not incur any additional measurement costs.

This study introduces Gromov Centrality, a multi-scale metric for assessing node centrality in graphs. Gromov Centrality quantifies the disparity between a node's Gromov distance from its surrounding area and the maximum possible distance (triangle inequality) within that region. The resulting metric exhibits key characteristics expected of a centrality measure: nodes with high centrality are connected to nodes that geodesically disperse rapidly. Furthermore, the Gromov Centrality distribution is unimodal, with a mode near zero. Notably, the metric can be computed efficiently, in linear or near-linear time, using modified versions of existing single-source shortest path algorithms. Our results showcase the Gromov Centrality's ability to capture meaningful patterns in various real-world networks.

This paper outlines the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravity (ASTG), an innovative approach to modeling static and dynamic gravitational fields. By employing a novel coordinate system, distinct from the conventional 3+3 4D system, ASTG offers simplified descriptions of various well-documented gravitational phenomena. The ASTG framework is built upon the Lorentz group, with the Azimuthal Angle (z) serving as a space coordinate, and a corresponding dual vector (B) functioning as a space-time entity. The resulting Stokes' theorem-based field equations provide unique insights into gravitational dynamics, with a stress-energy tensor (T) representing a combination of angular momentum and mass current density. The field equations themselves exhibit a distinctive structure, with a curvature vector (K) analogous to a refractive index in optics, and a curvature vector product tensor (Q) representing the spatial curvature of gravitational systems. Notably, the field equations reduce to the Poisson equation in the weak gravitational limit, and successfully reproduce the predictions of their dynamic counterpart in accordance with established experimental evidence.

The concept of rigorous equivalence for matrix pencils is extended, offering itself as a distinct equivalence relation. This newly defined relation yields various distinct classifications for collections of matrix pencils, with implications for structure preservation under linear combinations. This concept has significant implications in linear system theory and multivariable control.

We establish a general principle underlying the geometric aspects of T-duality by interpreting it as a dual equivalence of categories. This category equivalence relates two algebraic geometries, reflecting the concepts of twisted Poisson geometry and twisted torus homotopy types. Our approach, rooted in homotopy theory, provides novel insights into twisted tori. Additionally, we address the question of symmetry in T-duality by identifying cases in which the duality relationship exhibits symmetry.

We have developed a breakthrough method for embedding arbitrary finite metrics into planar metrics with a specific bound, based on the logarithm of the number of points and the maximum distance between them, with a specific constant. Our method also works for all graph metrics that do not contain a specific graph as a subgraph, and more generally for all graph metrics that do not contain a specific graph as a subgraph, with a specific bound, based on the logarithm of the number of points and the maximum distance between them, with a specific constant. A key step in our method involves the development of a new structural tool, specifically an $O(\log n)$-treewidth spanner for series-parallel graphs. Our method also works for all graph metrics that do not contain a specific graph as a subgraph, and more generally for all graph metrics that do not contain a specific graph as a subgraph, with a specific bound, based on the logarithm of the number of points and the maximum distance between them, with a specific constant.

In discrete-time systems, the smooth, strongly monotonic functions form an essential class for solving various optimization problems. However, existing research on the dynamic behavior of such systems remains relatively limited. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by classifying smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time systems into distinct categories based on their local and global stability properties, ultimately revealing the prevalence of unstable dynamics within this class. To support its findings, the paper employs tools from algebraic and complex analysis, as well as measures of volume, to demonstrate the prevalence of unstable discrete-time systems among smooth, strongly monotonic systems.

Quantum computers have significant potential in solving complex mathematical problems, but they have inherent limitations and require further research. To address these issues, the development of adaptive variational quantum eigensolvers is being investigated as a promising solution. This approach relies on a specific type of quantum circuit that can be adjusted based on the system being studied. Researchers have explored this method and found it effective for certain problems, but the limits of this approach are still unknown. A novel approach is proposed in the form of the qubit-excitation-driven adaptive variational quantum eigensolver, which prioritizes the most significant terms in the adaptive ansatz circuit based on the system's properties. This method is shown to be equivalent to a type of coupled cluster approach commonly used in chemistry. By testing this approach on a series of complex molecules, the researchers found the QEVQEA to be more accurate and efficient than previous methods, with significant advantages for modern quantum computers with limited circuit depth.

A common issue in neural representation learning arises from the difficulty in utilizing the information contained within the encoded representations. This challenge is particularly pronounced in the context of neural language modeling, where transformer models are widely used. In our research, we investigate the application of neural language modeling with convolutional and graph neural networks, employing masked autoencoders to learn representations from graph-structured sequences. However, the direct use of these representations as a basis for language modeling is hindered by their compressed nature. We propose a novel, lightweight approach to address this limitation, leveraging the final network layer to create a generative decoder that significantly enhances the quality of our language models, achieving substantial gains in downstream tasks, including grammar induction, generation, and prediction.

The Hubble tension could potentially be resolved by taking into account the impact of stochastic gravitational waves on Hubble parameter and age of the universe estimates. This type of gravitational wave background has been found to significantly affect the low-$\ell$ temperature polarization and 21cm power spectrum, as well as the Hubble parameter and age of the universe estimates, due to its energy density contribution. This background is generated by a dark matter field that temporarily decouples and re-couples with visible matter, and its amplitude and frequency are determined by the properties of the decoupling process.

Interferometric observations of the volatile gases emitted by comet C/2015 ER61, made using the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) at 112 and 89 GHz during its passage through the inner solar system, have been analyzed. Data collected in early 2017 revealed no significant H2O or CO emissions, but H2S was detected in the nucleus with an average brightness temperature of 1.85 K. Data also showed that H2S was not confined to the comet's central area. Observations indicated a possible point source of H2S, but the data was insufficient to confirm this. An alternative explanation, however, is that the observed H2S was spread out over a large area and the point source was an artifact of the data processing. Utilizing the ACA's high-resolution capabilities has enabled researchers to study the behavior of H2S in this comet, providing new insights into the composition and activity of cometary volatiles.

We propose an unsupervised approach to creating artificial speech without the need for explicit pronunciation annotations. Unlike most models that rely on specific mappings between text and speech data, our approach enables discovered connections to be bypassed for unrecognized words or phrases. We introduce a new unsupervised projection method that automatically identifies potential speech-text associations from text and speech-alone data, which is then used to train a text-to-speech model. Additionally, we propose an efficient single-speaker TTS system that processes and synthesizes audio at high speeds, processing approximately 100 words per second in both training and inference phases. We evaluate our method using the LUKE challenge benchmark dataset, demonstrating a significant reduction in Mean Opinion Score (MOS) between real and synthetic speech for the test set.

This article explores the effectiveness of Tsallis entropy as a viable approach within the context of the holographic principle. By employing the Schwarzschild-de Sitter horizon as a reference scale, we derive an expression for the thermal time required for a closed system to reach thermal equilibrium. Additionally, we investigate the impact of modifying the holographic entropy bound by introducing a complex form of the Ricci dark energy model. Our model, inspired by quintessence theory, involves replacing the standard Cosine function of the Ricci dark energy model with a complex form, specifically the Hyperbolic Cosine function. By comparing the present-day values of the statefinder diagnostic parameters ($r$ and $s$) in the modified models to their Ricci dark energy counterparts, we determine that the analyzed models are suitable alternatives to the original Ricci dark energy model.

Multi-objective Mixed Integer Non Linear Optimization problems are widespread in real-world applications and are investigated using two approaches: (a) converting a multi-objective problem into a single-objective problem and then solving it, and (b) utilizing Meta-heuristic algorithms such as NSGA-II to generate a Pareto front. The paper highlights the challenges in solving Multi-objective problems and discusses transformation-based and Meta-heuristic methods, before presenting numerical examples that illustrate the advantages and limitations of each approach.

We demonstrate that within the framework of synthetic differential geometry, linked Lie groupoids are 'inherently connected,' meaning that for any two points $x$ and $y$, $x$ can be expressed as a finite combination of equivalent points to $y$. This property also implies that the relation $\sim$ defined by the groupoid is an integer component of the general relation $\Lambda$ in terms of the connectedness structure, specifically, $q(\Lambda/x) = q(\sim/x)$ for the canonical map $q$. Notably, this concept of being an integer component differs from the more traditional definition, requiring only that for a surjective differential map $q$, the induced function $q/q^{-1}(x)$ is surjective, contrasting with the standard definition where $q/q^{-1}(x)$ is injective.

The rapid advancement of AI and machine learning techniques in medical research has been complemented by significant progress in medical imaging and clinical data collection technologies. Nevertheless, the critical challenge of ensuring the privacy and security of sensitive patient information during data transfer remains a significant concern. This study presents an innovative framework utilizing network function virtualization and software-defined networking through cyberinfrastructure gateways to facilitate secure data exchange between medical imaging systems and clinical platforms. This proposed solution allows for seamless data sharing while safeguarding patient privacy and promoting secure collaboration within medical research environments.

In Aspect Sentiment Analysis, classifying sentiment towards specific aspects, a particular sentiment type called implicit sentiment poses a significant challenge. Unlike explicit sentiment, which can be easily identified through sentiment indicators, implicit sentiment is more subtle and challenging to discern. To address this, we propose a pre-training approach called SILO, which utilizes supervised contrastive pre-training to capture implicit sentiment. Our strategy involves two key components: a natural language processing model that learns implicit sentiment through a supervised contrastive loss function, and a lightweight sentiment indicator that helps the model make informed predictions about implicit sentiment. Our pre-trained model is then fine-tuned for Aspect Sentiment Analysis, utilizing supervised contrastive pre-training with human sentiment labels and aspect labels from Amazon reviews. Our results on the Amazon dataset demonstrate that SILO achieves superior performance compared to previous state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its potential to effectively capture implicit sentiment towards specific aspects.

To evaluate the impact of policy changes, it's often necessary to understand how intermediate factors, or mediators, are influenced. In situations where the primary outcome, mediator, and auxiliary variables are all measurable, a specific computation can be used to determine total effects, provided certain assumptions hold true. A two-step process can be used to break down total effects into components based on changes in the initial variable and the mediator. However, when data is collected using case-control sampling, a particular step-circle control computation can be used to accurately account for this sampling method. In this context, a theoretical proof is provided to show that the mediation computation holds when the mediator is binary, and an alternative computational approach is formulated that relies on fewer assumptions. An accompanying simulation demonstrates the effectiveness of this theoretical proof in a range of scenarios.

This study proposes a robust multiuser transmission strategy for secure communication networks utilizing reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, despite defects in the power amplifiers. Specifically, we design precoding vectors that ensure the transmitted data remains secure and reliable for multiple receivers, even with the power amplifiers operating in their linear region, on a network featuring a RIS. By reconfiguring the RIS phase shifts, we optimize the network to compensate for the imperfections of the power amplifiers and maximize transmission security and reliability. A two-step optimization method is developed to efficiently compute the precoding vectors and phase shifts through convex optimization techniques. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of the proposed strategy in random hardware-impaired multiuser networks through numerical analysis.

We introduce a novel technique for augmenting conversation datasets by harnessing a unique language model's capacity to shift in perspective and label values through summarization. By simulating diverse viewpoints and subtly adjusting value orientations, our approach generates insightful, albeit fictional, summaries that enhance the diversity and depth of the conversation data. Building upon the capabilities of Resampling, our approach integrates these capabilities with its own perspective-shifting capabilities, thereby streamlining the data enhancement process. Moreover, our technique demonstrates a significant resistance to biases and inconsistencies in the generated content. Through thorough evaluation processes, our approach showcases the value of fictional summaries that contribute to the overall quality and depth of the conversation data.

The solar breeze, a type of plasma flow, is the primary component of the heliosphere's interior. To study the solar breeze, we analyzed data collected by Parker Solar Probe during six close encounters with the sun, utilizing electric fields, magnetic fields, and plasma measurements. By examining these data, we created a model of the solar breeze's magnetic field and energy flow patterns, and identified key characteristics, including magnetic signatures, energy cascade, and dissipation. Our investigation revealed that, at close ranges to the sun, magnetic fields exhibit significant fluctuations, which decrease as distance from the sun increases, which is in line with in-situ solar breeze observations. Moreover, our model indicates that magnetic energy tends to dissipate at larger distances, which is caused by current sheets associated with larger-scale structures, which is an expected outcome of turbulent cascades. Our model also shows that the solar breeze's magnetic field exhibits a consistent pattern of energy cascade and magnetic dissipation, which begins at smaller scales and extends to larger scales.

In a noncommutative setting, a construction is developed for a family of equivariant principal bundles over locally compact Hausdorff G-space X, which extends to noncommutative G-C*-algebras A, yielding a principal G-bundle π: ℘ → X, centered on a G-action on ℘. For a specific case involving the Cantor set as the G-space and the Cantor group as G, it is demonstrated that there is an equivalence between Cantor set C bundles and free actions of Cantor group ℘, as well as a method for constructing Canton set bundles using pullbacks. Furthermore, certain bundles over the Cantor set are shown to have free group actions, along with determinations of their equivariant K-theory and Ko-theory.

In the realm of infinite cardinal arithmetic, specifically concerning the continuum, we examine two key invariants: $\mathfrak u$, which represents the minimal size of a maximal almost disjoint family of subsets of $\omega$, and $\mathfrak d$, which is the minimal size of a dominating family within $\omega^\omega$. The study aims to gain insights into the nature of $\mathfrak u$ by analyzing its relationship with $\mathfrak d$ and other cardinals within this domain. To this end, we begin by introducing the concept of the quasi-ordering $\le_{fin}^*$ on $[\omega]^\omega$, defined as $A \le_{fin}^* B$ if the set $\{n \in \omega : |A \cap [0,n]| - |B \cap [0,n]|| > n$ is finite, and subsequently show the equivalence of the cardinality of the filter $\mathfrak u$ to the cofinality of the dominating number $\mathfrak d$ under the assumption that $\mathfrak u$ is a prime ideal. Furthermore, we introduce the cardinality $\mathfrak d^*$ associated with the filter $\mathfrak d$, and demonstrate its relationship with the cardinality $\mathfrak u$ based on whether $\mathfrak d^*$ dominates $\mathfrak u$ or is dominated by $\mathfrak u$.
