This article presents the customisation of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, specifically the question-answer variant using the DPR retriever, to function within the legal domain. We examine the performance of the DPR framework, incorporating the legal knowledge base, with both an existing question-answer model and a domain-specific question-answer model, which was trained on an annotated dataset of questions and answers derived from an article. Our research indicates that the fine-tuned RAG framework, in conjunction with the DPR retriever, exhibits superior performance in question-answer evaluation, outperforming the baseline generated by the unmodified RAG framework, when assessed using the QAC evaluation metric.

This study derives a limiting differential equation for a sequence of polynomials $\{P_n\}$ that are orthogonal relative to the function $\log \frac{1}{|x|}$ on the interval $[-1,1]$. By employing a method proposed by J. Humpert and M. Petkovic, we employ a change of variables and a corresponding transformation of the differential equation. In the process, we discover that the limiting equation is a Bessel-type equation, and we also obtain a discrete zeros theorem for this type of equation, thereby enabling us to confirm that the polynomials $\{P_n\}$ are oscillatory within the given interval.

This research explores the intricacies of identifying top-tier annotators for complex summarization tasks, which is often overlooked. A series of interactions with 10 diverse participants, who annotated a subset of the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, revealed that annotators' quality is significantly influenced by their level of motivation, familiarity with the task, and ability to interpret ambiguous instructions. Notably, the majority of the 70 additional annotators selected randomly exhibited subpar quality, underscoring the necessity of refining the process of identifying high-quality annotators.

Text-video retrieval systems, which depend on comprehensive video and textual feature extraction, have been extensively researched. The latest method employs the Transformer's Self-Attention mechanism, allowing for more flexible feature interaction. However, this approach can lead to increased computational complexity and memory usage, particularly when processing long sequences. To address this limitation, we developed a novel architecture called Token Shift and Choice Transformer (TS2-Net), incorporating Transformer-BERT's sequential token shifting mechanism and adding a Self-Attention module selectively activated by a binary mask generated by a following transformer module. This design significantly reduces computation and memory requirements, offering better efficiency and adaptability. Experimental results on RTE and TREC datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach, achieving impressive performance with RTE (72.2%) and TREC (70.0%) metrics, while surpassing the existing baseline by a substantial 2.6% in TV-Attn.

We propose that neutral currents which change a top quark into a bottom or charm quark can arise due to the existence of a heavy neutral scalar boson that decays into a neutrino and dark matter particle. The dark matter density constraint is used to estimate the magnitude of a specific coupling, which in turn is translated into the standard model framework using effective field theory, resulting in novel predictions for $t\to b$ and $t\to c$ transitions that are potentially testable in future $t\bar{t}$ production at the LHC.

This study introduces a family of directed hybrid network models, combining preferential attachment and uniform random networks, which, according to recent findings, exhibit an distribution of out-degrees following a power-law law. These networks, which, based on a hybrid model proposed by Bafalou et al., simultaneously capture the complexity of preferential attachment and uniform random networks, allow the investigation of various physical properties. The analysis demonstrates that the resulting network is connected with high probability and characterizes the distribution of path lengths between nodes. The study also provides an evaluation of the distribution of out-degrees and examines the evolution of the network size over time. Furthermore, it assesses the complexity of finding a shortest path between nodes. The analysis of these model networks, which, as an extension of a model proposed by Bafalou et al., is directed, has significant implications for understanding directed networks.

A new Multi-Labell Disturbance Detection (MLDD) framework is introduced, 
expanding on the capabilities of traditional single-task disturbance detection.
This framework can accurately identify and distinguish between various forms of
machine disturbances in addition to their presence or absence using images as input.
To this end, we have created a multi-labeled dataset consisting of a variety of
machine disturbance scenarios drawn from diverse sources, and have developed a
Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture to distinguish these multiple
labels simultaneously. Our findings demonstrate that the MLDD approach is feasible
and can be effectively implemented using existing Source Separation and Classification
(SCC) systems by training the CNN classifier with multiple labels, thereby improving
disturbance classification accuracy. Furthermore, in scenarios where a machine's audio
signal is obscured by noise or other disturbances, the MLDD framework can still 
correctly identify the running machine's presence even when these disturbances are not 
simultaneously classified.

Displacement in spatial dimensions may be a natural aspect that arises from the altered geometry structure following the addition of a magnetic field. This concept is exemplified by Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic strings, which have a unique structure combining displacement and a helical nature. The displacement parameter in this case corresponds to a specific angle. This work investigates the relationships between energy, charge, and vorticity in the context of Klein-Gordon particles within the Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic string spacetime. Furthermore, it explores how the displacement parameter and electric field influence the observed relationships between the particle's spin and orbital degrees of freedom.

This paper demonstrates that the algebra of real measurable sets with cardinality greater than $\aleph_0$ possesses a sub-algebra that is isomorphic to the measurability structure, $M$, defined in the introduction. The theorem establishing this conclusion relies heavily on a critical lemma that might be useful in other contexts as well. Additionally, it is shown that for every locale algebra, $\mathcal{B}$, its maximal homomorphic image is isomorphic to the locale algebra, $M$, defined in the introduction, provided that $\mathcal{B}$'s cardinality is greater than $\aleph_0$.

Measuring the alignment of the electron and proton after the electron scattering process in DVCS is crucial for understanding the photon's interaction with quarks and gluons, providing insights into spin-dependent parton distributions. The electron alignment can be determined through its energy and angle measurements in the detector, while the proton alignment is obtained from its azimuthal angle after the scattering process. The relationship between these measurements can be expressed as $\vec{e'}\cdot \vec{p'} = \cos\gamma$, with $\gamma$ representing the determined angle in the experimental setup. The DVCS cross section is proportional to $\cos\gamma$, allowing the reconstruction of the proton alignment from multiple events in the detector. The $\gamma$ variable offers a clear distinction between the interferential and beam-dependent parts of the DVCS cross section, providing a clear separation of the $S_{1T}$ and $S_{1C}$ terms. The $\gamma$ variable offers a clear distinction between $S_{1C}/F_2$ and $F_L$ in terms of magnitude, and the $S_{1T}/F_2$ term dominates the $\mathcal{A}_U^\perp$ observable. The $\gamma$ variable offers a clear distinction between $S_{1T}/F_2$ and $S_{1C}/F_2$ in terms of sign, and the $\gamma$ observable offers a clear distinction between $S_{1T}/F_2$

I'm examining the growing significance of artificial intelligence in society and its practical applications, which are now considered essential tools. I'm evaluating the current state of AI and its limitations, which are now apparent. I'm exploring ways to enhance AI capabilities, drawing on human cognitive abilities, and I'm also considering societal implications and the management of advanced AI systems. These concepts will be applied to solve real-world problems, such as those in the energy sector.

In this research, we explore the behavior of bosons with spin-orbit connections in a lattice system, considering both experimental and theoretical aspects. We focus on a specific scenario within this context, utilizing the tight-binding model, where we examine the superfluid phase diagram that emerges when temperature and interaction strength vary. We discover that the first-order thermal phase transition, which occurs at low temperatures, undergoes a second-order transition at higher temperatures and stronger interactions. Additionally, the critical thermal shift's dependence on the experimentally accessible spin-orbit coupling strength's parameter is relatively moderate across all boson interaction strengths.

Graph theory and the application of groups to graphs have been extensively studied for over 50 years, with an emphasis on their various relationships and transformations. This focus has led to the study of a broad class of equivalence relations, known as group rewrites, that describe how groups can be transformed into new groups with different properties. A notable subset of these rewrites, known as degradations, involves non-trivial group homomorphisms and provide a way to understand the structural limitations of groups within the class. This paper aims to explore the characteristics of these degradations, including their relationship with group kernels, images, and the development of universal groups, with an examination of specific cases and their implications for the overall field.

This study explores various aspects of the AdS/CFT correspondence, particularly concerning low-dimensional theories. We examined the interactions of D0-D4-D4-D4 BPS states in the type II A limit using the open string formalism, and discovered AdS$_5$/CFT$_5$ corresponds to N=4 superconformal symmetry in the plasma state, where BPS states can map to superconformal primary states, suggesting the possibility of describing plasma primary states via open string formalism. We also investigated the BPS properties of a light open string and proposed that it corresponds to the BPS state of a specific light mode in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, after including the effects of the compactified internal space. Additionally, we studied the BPS properties of a stringy configuration involving a string and a Wilson line in AdS$_5$ through the open string and probe D-brane formalism, and derived BPS conditions for configurations with finite or infinite Wilson lines, ultimately leading to the discovery of new BPS conditions and an extension of previous results.

The ability to handle uncertainty is a crucial aspect of machine learning, with the ability to balance exploration and exploitation. Gaussian Processes (GP) are widely recognized for their unique capacity to do this, thanks to the flexibility of GP kernels in adjusting their behavior. This study focuses on a new class of kernels, known as trigonometric kernels, which are a direct result of a specific mathematical equation, and demonstrates their potential through practical applications. By exploring varying regimes, these kernels can effectively switch between a stationary and non-stationary processes, which are typically modeled separately. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that a combination of sinusoidal components in the mathematical expression leads to GPs with a stationary covariance structure, characterized by a spectral density that can be tailored to a specific set of target frequencies. By adjusting a single parameter, this process can be used to match the spectral density of a standard Mat\'ern kernel, which is a common choice in GP modeling.

Achieving beam-induced noise (BIM) mitigation at high-energy muon colliders is a critical challenge for a successful experiment. This paper explores various methods to reduce beam-induced noise on muon colliders, including strategies for a high-luminosity muon collider based on CaF$_3$ scintillator technology and their application to other materials.

We propose a novel regularization technique, Sparsity-R, which leverages a non-differentiable, convex and monotonic function to control various forms of sparsity, encompassing element-wise, matrix, tensor, and graph data. By integrating this dynamic regularization, we enable adaptive control of sparsity in data with complex hierarchies and connections. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods on tasks involving imaged data with structured sparsity, specifically in medical image reconstruction and face part detection.

A key feature of fermions is their inability to occupy the same two-particle state, known as the Pauli obstruction. This phenomenon is typically observed in strongly interacting systems, but in this study, it is found to arise in a weakly interacting Bose fluid when considering specific temperature and density conditions. Using a model based on Bogoliubov excitations, the research demonstrates that fermionic states experience exclusion even when not taking into account correlations, and this effect is not solely due to antisymmetry. Notably, the phenomenon is not confined to bosons and also occurs in systems with different types of excitations.

A key aspect of software quality is a pleasant smell, characterized by well-written code that adheres to established best practices, according to the renowned mantra by Fowler and Beck. Conversely, research suggests that bad-smelling software is often associated with structural issues, making it vital to investigate the connection between such issues and olfactory qualities. Our study challenges this notion by proposing an alternative perspective, where the clean smell of software is merely a superficial resemblance to well-structured, maintainable code, and we provide empirical evidence from a real-world setting to support this claim. Our research was conducted through a systematic investigation of the perspectives of software developers regarding the significance of these odors, and we gathered insights from a diverse group of 20 Java developers, and the results indicate that developers are motivated to eliminate bad-smelling code to enhance their workflow, and we discuss the potential implications of our findings.

This paper introduces a general framework for solving dynamic optimization problems, which includes finding the equilibrium state of a complex system. These problems can be mathematically formulated using nonconvex vector-valued integrals that involve images of continuous sweeping procedures. These images can exist in a high-dimensional space or on a surface. To address the challenge posed by nonconvexity, a new approach is presented, which generalizes both the convex-sweeping theorem and the Brouwer fixed-point theorem. This generalized approach is then applied to several complex systems, including those found in economics, traffic modeling, and pattern formation.

The KKMCee program, a newly updated version of the well-known KKMC, is designed for simulating lepton colliders. It accounts for multiple photon emissions at various orders in quantum electrodynamics theory. This simulation program is crucial for creating realistic event data and assessing the performance of lepton colliders. In the process of simulating electron-positron collisions to produce quarks or leptons, a large number of photons are typically emitted due to the strong interaction between quarks or final state quark color charges. Photons are simulated using the structure functions Lrva and Zrva for both initial and final state radiation. These functions are then combined with standard structure functions for initial state radiation to produce a complete event description.

Determining inter-beat intervals (IBs) is a crucial step in analyzing heart beat patterns, particularly for identifying irregularities and anomalies. This research presents a novel method for IB interval estimation, which involves utilizing EmbezzoTiramizo algorithms to extract IBs from audio-based heart beat signals. The Embezzo and Tiramizo algorithms, being part of a larger family known as Embezzo and Tiramizo, are designed to analyze complex systems and detect patterns. The Embezzo algorithm compresses the IB time series, while the Tiramizo algorithm identifies the points of change in the compressed data. Our method involves detecting heart beat points using the Tiramizo algorithm and evaluating their accuracy on a large dataset. We also conducted experiments to compare our approach with other IB interval estimation methods, such as Euclidean distance and dynamic time warping. The results show that our method is effective in improving the accuracy of IB interval estimation and reducing error rates. Our method has the potential to significantly advance the understanding of heart beat patterns and improve the diagnosis of heart-related diseases.

To process massive datasets efficiently, parallel and distributed computing platforms are often employed. However, traditional tensor singular value decomposition (tSVD) methods require the entire dataset to be stored in memory, rendering them impractical for tensors exceeding the available memory. This study introduces a stochastic method for tSVD that processes and analyzes the tensor in a single pass, making it feasible to utilize on such computing systems with limited memory. Furthermore, after analyzing the stochastic iteration's properties, we discovered that convergence can be determined without assessing the entire tensor, thus allowing for efficient computation even on platforms with insufficient memory.

Embedding dynamic networks is crucial for various graph data analysis tasks.
Existing methods focus on static graphs and do not capture their temporal nature.
To address this, we examine how temporal characteristics of dynamic graphs change
over time and propose an approach that yields a low-dimensional time series for
each node in the graph. We also develop two dynamic node embedding models based
on short-term and long-term temporal dependencies. Experimental results on
synthetic and real-world datasets show that our approach outperforms existing
methods in embedding accuracy and provides effective nodes' temporal features.

To investigate the properties of very neutron-rich nuclei, the Multi-Nucleon Transfer Reaction (MNT) has been utilized. A specific study focused on $^7$H, where the reaction $^{10}$B($^4$He, $^3$H) $^7$H was examined at a centroid energy of 5.8 MeV/nucleon. A notable feature in the $^3$H spectrum suggested the population of $^7$H's ground state, corresponding to the $^3$H + 4n excitation. A detailed study of the angular distribution revealed a structure in the $^7$H ground state, interpreted as the $^3$H + 4n excitation. This was supported by a calculated binding energy of $-1.47\pm 0.28$ MeV for $^7$H and a half-life of 1.3 fs. A theoretical model using the Jost function, combined with the experimental data, revealed that $^7$H's ground state, with spin-parity 1/2+, has a virtual resonance with energy $E_R=-0.84\pm 0.14$ MeV and a width of 0.44 MeV. This resonance, with spin-parity 3/2+, is believed to be the excited state of $^7$H populated in the $^6$H+n
The Nirenberg issue for the half spheres presents a non-trivial blow-up problem.

This study investigates the use of Wasserstein distances in optimal representation learning by employing them as the loss function in neural networks. Our research indicates that the hierarchical nature of Sinkhorn distances enables the creation of network representations with inherent depth, effectively replacing traditional layered structures. We introduce neural networks that learn via sequential minimization of increasingly larger Sinkhorn distances, dubbed depth-acquiring neural networks (DANNs). We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

The local tracing collaborations in the UK, where residents are directed to use
separate tracing services depending on their previous health history, pose potential
issues with the overall contact tracing strategy. To evaluate their effect on
contact tracing efficiency, the ONS developed a mathematical model of the COVID-19
spread, factoring in tracing collaborations, to simulate the model's behavior and
determine their impact on efficiency. The results show that the current policy of
local tracing collaborations significantly reduces the effectiveness of contact
tracing in the UK. Specifically, implementing these collaborations could decrease
contact tracing efficiency by up to 20%, equating to approximately 10 additional
infections per day. To mitigate this, local tracing collaborations should be
redesigned to ensure seamless data exchange between services, thus maximizing
contact tracing effectiveness.

Researchers have conducted an in-depth analysis of the open cluster Melotte 72, located at a distance of 2.13 kpc, using the Gaia DR2 dataset. By cross-referencing dataset information, they determined the cluster's center to be at a specific sky position. Utilizing isochrone fitting, the team calculated the cluster's age to be 2.0 billion years and derived its heliocentric velocity. Results indicate the cluster's proper motion values and its current estimated age. Additionally, the study determined the cluster's position in space, revealing it to be located at a galactic latitude and longitude. Utilizing 2MASS data, the team resolved the cluster's main sequence and constructed a color-magnitude diagram, which allowed them to calculate the classical and re-calculated values for the Sun's metallicity. Furthermore, the team calculated the total mass of the cluster, derived the mass function exponent, and determined the binary fraction within the cluster.

This study examines the Betti numbers of Gaussian distributions when the proportion of active components is very small. Building on previous findings, we demonstrate that under a specific scenario, the first Betti number of such distributions has a specific large-scale expectation and variance. Furthermore, we establish bounds on the second Betti number and provide an estimate for its typical magnitude.

This paper addresses the challenge of calibrating intrinsics and pose parameters for eye-in-hand cameras. Given a monocular image, we simultaneously determine the camera's pose and its parameters. To achieve this, we represent the camera's degrees of freedom as the coordinates of five key points on a six-point sphere. Our proposed method leverages a pre-trained deep learning model to estimate these key points. To ensure accurate self-supervision, we develop a novel loss function that accounts for the interdependence of the key points, their positions, and the camera's intrinsic parameters. Our experiments confirm the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating successful recovery of the camera's pose and parameters from unsupervised image datasets.

A widely accepted principle in control theory, often called the "reverse causality principle," suggests that if a variable has an impact on another's outcome, then altering the first variable can influence the second's result. However, this rule doesn't always hold when dealing with hidden factors. This paper focuses on a specific scenario where the relationship between two variables is obscured by an unmeasured variable, but the underlying framework is such that this unmeasured factor cannot be directly affected by any possible manipulation. This context arises frequently in practical applications, including medical research and behavioral studies. This paper outlines a novel method, reverse constrained reinforcement training (RCRT), for determining the optimal strategy to achieve a specific outcome, given that some controlling variables are inaccessible. The proposed RCRT method is grounded in a dual optimization formulation, which enables the incorporation of constraints directly into the problem. This, in turn allows for efficient solutions to complex problems, including constrained linear and quadratic problems, to be addressed analytically. This paper also includes a concise explanation of the reasoning behind the impact of the derived constraints and presents numerical examples to demonstrate the impact of the identified constraints.

The Galaxy Mappping with the GAIA space telescope is set to significantly enhance our understanding of the Milky Way's structure and evolution, as well as the dynamics of nearby galaxies. A vast amount of data will be gathered from a trillion-star survey, utilizing photometry, astrometry, and spectral classification, along with radial velocity measurements. This comprehensive dataset will be instrumental in unraveling the intricacies of stellar populations, planetary systems, and the galaxy's past, present, and future, providing invaluable insights into the evolution of the Milky Way.

We have developed an efficient polynomial-time algorithm, specifically running in $\tilde{O}(n^2)$, to transform any n-vertex graph into a tree-decomposition where the tree width is half-logarithmically bounded. In this tree-decomposition, the graph can be partitioned into subgraphs via a binary tree structure, where each branch is separated by a single vertex and complies with both tree and separation constraints. This new algorithm significantly outperforms the previously established $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ bound by Nagl and Spanjers and is further optimized when considering the graph's separator size, running in $\tilde{O}(n + s^2)$, where s denotes the separator size.

The application of weights in networks has been widely utilized across various fields, offering a versatile tool for capturing complex relationships between entities. We examine the implications of positive and negative weights in the context of inferred and observed networks where directionality is also considered. We identify specific interpretations for each weight type and discuss the essential requirements for their validity. We emphasize the importance of distinguishing between inferred and observed networks to avoid confusion and ensure clarity in understanding network structures. We also discuss some common weighting methods and highlight specific challenges associated with inference-based networks.

To ensure reliable use of neural network surrogates, particularly those incorporating physical principles to model complex phenomena, we establish a framework for quantifying the accuracy of these models after training. By incorporating constraints based on physical laws, our methodology ensures networks produce results within reliable boundaries, free from violations of these laws. We adapt the concept of a posterior error estimation from traditional numerical methods to trained neural networks, enabling estimation of actual errors based on verified predictions. Our approach involves developing an error metric that evaluates a network's output against a simpler verification equation, thus facilitating an error estimate. To validate this method, we apply it to two different layers of physics-informed neural networks and discover that more intricate equations yield larger errors. Furthermore, we ensure that trained networks meet minimum accuracy standards by retraining them if necessary.

Airborne pathogens can cause diseases such as tuberculosis, influenza, and COVID-19 by dispersing through the air, posing significant risks in confined spaces. Recent research has focused on predicting the risks of these diseases based on environmental factors, with some studies using advanced machine learning and AI models. This paper aims to review and summarize existing models for assessing airborne contamination in such settings, with a focus on the application of geostatistics and AI in risk prediction. It will also highlight the limitations of current models and suggest potential future research directions to improve the accuracy of these predictions.

To differentiate between zero-bias peaks arising from Majorana modes and other types of peaks, it's necessary to establish a reliable experimental technique. Since there isn't a well-established method yet, we suggest an experiment that involves tunneling spectroscopy with an additional inductance in the superconductor. This proposed experiment includes replacing the usual tunneling electrode with a high-permeability material to induce a unique non-linear resistance characteristic. The results indicate that the presence of inductance in the superconductor leads to the suppression of Majorana-related zero-bias peaks due to the lack of a stable phase, while other types of zero-bias peaks remain stable. Furthermore, our simulations reveal the potential to identify these different peaks based on the zero-bias conductance's behavior in response to changes in inductance and coupling between the superconductor and inductance.

The straightforward multi-armed bandit problem, though having a well-established solution, is still a source of debate when it comes to theoretical guarantees in finite scenarios. Our study builds upon previous research concerning action diversity in linear bandits, focusing on diverse action sets that can be represented as elements within a geometric lattice. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of finite bandit algorithms compared to their infinite counterparts, and, conversely, highlight the detrimental effects of removing action diversity on the convergence rate of finite bandit algorithms. Our simulations reveal a significant decrease in performance when removing diversity, and,,,, highlighting a crucial consideration for real-world applications where diversity may be compromised due to design or maintenance issues, thus rendering our results applicable to cold-start problems and other challenges involving inference.

Graphene with gaps has potential applications in developing graphene-based quantum computers, with effects that can be utilized to read out and manipulate valley degrees of freedom. In this research, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect in graphene with gaps can serve as an effective means of valence and conduction band carriers separation. Through numerical calculations, we find that gap size and chemical potential influence the value of the orbital Hall conductivity, suggesting that this phenomenon has potential in orbital Hall insulators for creating efficient graphene devices that manipulate and detect valley degrees of freedom.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at solving complex graph classification tasks but are susceptible to being deceived by strategically crafted adversarial inputs. While existing research has focused on generating adversarial examples for existing trained models, we explore a novel scenario where an adversary can influence the learning process itself by introducing manipulated data to a training dataset. We称 this type of influence as data contamination attacks. To investigate this phenomenon, we developed an adversarial reinforcement learning framework that generates optimal actions to contamine the training data of both message passing GNNs and graph GAutoEncoder-based GNNs. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which can compromise both node classification and link prediction performance, especially when the attacker has a significant portion of the training data to manipulate, achieving up to 90% classification accuracy.

The problem of matching entries across different astronomical catalogs is addressed by developing a novel algorithm that leverages the relative positions and distances of celestial objects, as well as their brightness levels. A catalog-embedding technique based on a clustering method is presented, allowing for the assessment of catalog item similarity through observed astrometric and photometric data. A performance evaluation of the proposed algorithm reveals that it outperforms existing solutions, as substantiated by experiments on benchmark datasets.

Incountable edge hypergraphs with edge symmetry, such that a set of edges can cover all edges given by an infinite hypergraph, are explored in relation to a conjecture proposed by Erdos. Specifically, it is proven that such minimal edge covers exist in these hypergraphs and their covers can be edgeless for certain cases. Furthermore, the results can be applied to a combinatorial problem, revealing the existence of minimal edge covers in symmetric hypergraphs with specific properties, where the covers can be as large as half of the vertices under certain conditions.

OntoPlot is an innovative visualization tool designed for navigating and visualizing large ontology networks, specifically tailored for applications like semantic web knowledge bases and biomedical systems. Traditional ontology visualizations struggle with complex structures, specifically those with hidden hierarchies, which are common in fields such as medicine and biology. OntoPlot addresses this limitation with its unique 3D visualization and hierarchical camera control features, which streamline the viewing process and highlight class relationships more effectively than flat or 2D alternatives. Its practicality is demonstrated with a detailed biomedical case study involving the extensive UMLS meta-ontology, comprising over 52 million instances.

This study explores a semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, focusing on improving performance through cross-domain transfer learning. A new inter-domain penalty function is introduced to facilitate this process, and the effect of acoustical model parameter initialization on performance is investigated. By utilizing the LS-PEM model, transducer ASR systems achieve up to 4.1 percentage point character error rate reduction on the Vox1b dataset, and it is observed that the model's performance is highly dependent on the LS-PEM model size and the ASR model initialization method employed.

A fundamental challenge in robotics involves enabling robots to move autonomously through their surroundings. Developing active inference methods for robot navigation has been a long-standing goal, but current approaches often fail to be universally applicable across diverse environments. We present Profound Active Inference, an advanced navigation strategy that allows an robot to plan a path to a target location based on a hierarchical structure of movement policies. When encountering an obstacle, the robot automatically adjusts its posture and can also adapt to unfamiliar environments using domain-specific knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate that this method provides a robust and scalable solution for robot navigation.

A soft sphere fluid, which has flexible molecules that can move freely, exhibits a unique behavior where it responds differently to external temperature gradients compared to the standard hard spheres. We've mathematically studied the Soret effect within this simple model and discovered that this softness in molecular structure actually amplifies the Soret effect, as opposed to the typical rigid bodies. Notably, this phenomenon arises from changes in how the molecules interact and organize themselves due to their elasticity, as opposed to the conventional molecular movement. Furthermore, this effect becomes more pronounced as the spongy core within the model's structure becomes more pronounced, which could potentially explain the Soret effect observed in biological systems and gels.

Recent advancements in automated document composition have been substantial, yet the models' performance is often evaluated using unreliable metrics. To address this issue, we propose a more effective evaluation method based on the MDeBERTa model, which delivers high results on a variety of benchmark tasks. Unlike traditional model-based metrics, our approach leverages MDeBERTa's capabilities to accurately assess the meaning and coherence of composed texts through similarity and anomaly detection. To validate the efficacy of our method, we conducted a large-scale experiment involving 50 participants who evaluated composed texts using our model-based metric and actual human ratings. The results demonstrate a substantial correlation between our model and human ratings across multiple evaluation dimensions, thereby confirming its reliability. Furthermore, our research reveals that existing state-of-the-art metrics fail to accurately reflect human ratings, whereas our proposed MDeBERTa model achieves a notably higher correlation.

In practical situations, the issue of false positives is a significant challenge in the field of domain adaptive pedestrian identification. A proposed approach involves re-evaluating the re-ranking process to identify and eliminate false positives. The concept of box re-ranking has been introduced to address this problem by focusing on the bounding boxes associated with each detection candidate rather than just the images. The box re-ranking method involves matching the features of pedestrian detections with their corresponding bounding boxes to resolve ambiguities among top identification results that have fallen below a certain threshold. Unlike conventional re-ranking techniques that rely on handcrafted features, the proposed approach leverages pre-trained neural networks to extract features, thereby reducing the need for manual feature design. The proposed method does not require any labeled data for re-ranking purposes, distinguishing it from other unsupervised methods such as hard-matching and hard-re-ranking. The effectiveness of the proposed approach has been demonstrated through extensive experiments on the CityPersons dataset, where it has achieved state-of-the-art performance, particularly in mitigating false positives and achieving a significant reduction of 22.9% in false positive rates, outperforming existing unsupervised methods like hard-matching.

This research introduces a novel approach to text-to-speech synthesis, which combines image conversion and vocoding techniques. Our method involves training a text-to-image model and an image-to speech model, which leads to it in a more controllable and efficient manner compared to traditional text-to-speech methods. The separation of acoustic information into an intermediate visual representation enables the use of a smaller, simpler acoustic-to-speech mapping, which can be achieved with a smaller network. Our proposed approach demonstrates better speech quality with more diverse speech patterns using small datasets and demonstrates reduced AUR in boundaries. Additionally, it offers greater control over speech synthesis through the use of an intermediate visual representation.

Our ability to throw objects accurately and strategically is crucial in activities such as sports, military operations, and daily tasks. However, mistakes inevitably occur, prompting a crucial question: how do we correct our aim when the point of release is incorrect? This research investigates the mechanisms by which humans adjust their throwing movements when the point of release is inaccurate. Using a novel experimental setup, we examined how participants adapted to errors in their throwing movements. Our experiment involved participants interacting with a virtual character that threw a ball with incorrect aim, and we analyzed the participants' corrective movements in two distinct scenarios: when the point of release was unknown and when it was visible. Our results indicate that participants exhibited more pronounced corrections when the point of release was visible, suggesting that visual feedback plays a crucial role in the correction process. Additionally, our research highlights the differences between our throwing movement model and previous models proposed by other researchers. Our findings contribute to our understanding of the throwing movement and its underlying mechanisms, and they have significant implications for the development of robotic throwing systems.

This study introduces a novel machine translation model that incorporates a syntax-driven decoding process, where a separate syntax parser generates potential syntax diagrams, and a selection mechanism chooses the most suitable diagram to guide further generation. The syntax-aware model, known as Neuronodal, integrates a pointer mechanism to selectively incorporate phrases from the selected diagram, producing more grammatically structured translations. Experimental results, particularly in Turkish-to-English translation, demonstrate that Neuronodal outperforms traditional models, particularly in maintaining structured syntax. The model also reveals that effective parsers, when used to select diagrams, yield substantial improvements. Notably, Neuronodal produces detailed syntax diagrams not required for translation but beneficial for understanding sentence structure, making it a valuable resource for syntactic analysis.

A novel database, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BAP), has been created to offer a comprehensive collection of quantum chemical binding energy data for a range of molecules of astrochemical significance, including those of interstellar carbon chemistry and nitrogen-bearing interstellar molecules. The BAP database features 180 dimers and 24 triplets, encompassing various anionic, cationic, and neutral species. Each binding energy value represents the interaction between a carbon-based monomer and an adsorbate, whether it be a carbon, nitrogen, or water molecule. Furthermore, the BAP database includes information on Adsorption Energy Isomers (AIs), a crucial factor in adsorption-reaction processes within astrochemical contexts. The platform's data is accessible via its website and an accompanying API, enabling users to explore Adsorption Energy Isomers, compare them with experimental data, and obtain adsorption energy distributions for exo- and endo- sites on various adsorbent surfaces.

This study focuses on the statistical analysis of a multiplicative stochastic process restricted to positive values, which corresponds to the continuous-time counterpart of the lattice process previously analyzed in our earlier work. We have identified and documented the effects of the minimum value limit on key properties of this process, such as its probability distribution function, which are also illustrated using simulations. Additionally, we have developed and evaluated potential applications of this process in modeling time series data and considered our findings in the context of relevant literature on multiplicative processes.

We propose a new method to quantify quantum circuit expectations using only single-shot measurements of measurement outcomes from shallow Clifford circuits. Unlike earlier techniques, which necessitate numerous shots per circuit, our approach requires a substantial number of shots for each circuit, but only one shot across all circuits. To achieve this, our method involves collecting an extensive dataset from all circuits, requiring more qubits and gates than previous approaches. To address the challenge of using only single-shot measurements, our method employs a model that accounts for distribution parameters derived from random Clifford circuits. To assess expectation values, our shallow shades method utilizes these distribution parameters, which are obtained from these low-depth random Clifford circuits. Our shallow shades method is shown to be effective through numerical simulations involving circuits of up to 20 qubits.

The reflection coefficient's asymptotic behavior as $z\to\infty$ is examined for the Davey-Stewartson II system, considering the case where the potential function lacks square integrability. For specific non-square integrable cases ($e^{2ik^{2}x}$ and $1/(1+e^{-x})$), assuming specific decay conditions for the potential, the asymptotic formula for the reflection coefficient, which includes the term $r(k) \sim \frac{1}{|k|}$, is derived for the $L^2$ scattering problem. This result resolves the ambiguity regarding the $|k|$ behavior of the reflection coefficient, which was previously unknown.

This study focuses on determining the degree to which text categorization systems remain consistent when presented with varying sets of reliable sources. Various methods have been applied to minimize the impact of unreliable sources, but these methods do not consider the reliability of sources. Our approach, text categorization robustness, assesses how much classification results change when text categorization systems are exposed to different sets of reliable sources. Four methods have been proposed to introduce variation in the source reliability, aiming to measure domain-specific categorization systems' robustness. Our findings indicate that our method effectively evaluates the reliability and variability of categorization systems, revealing a stronger correlation between robustness and the accuracy of unbiased systems compared to the mover's correlation.

A new, fully automatic method has been developed to lower the barrier for
artificial intelligence systems to learn from a variety of tasks efficiently.
This system, called Meta-IL, is capable of learning how to convert complex,
high-level concepts into simpler, visual representations similar to human
instructors. When presented with new tasks, it then uses reinforcement
learning to train an image classifier. This collaborative training process
enables the system to handle an almost infinite range of tasks, as it doesn't
rely on creating multiple datasets for each one. By leveraging this
cooperative training approach, the system can ensure that its model remains
transparent and trustworthy, and remains effective even when the complexity of
linear representations increases. This research presents the first fully
automated method that allows AI systems and human instructors to collaborate
on linear visualization creation, and the results demonstrate the efficacy of
this approach, showcasing the models it has generated on a variety of complex
datasets.

In recent years, multiple machine translation models have been proposed to enhance the performance of translation models with limited resources and knowledge, particularly those based on extraction and quantization. This study evaluates the resilience of these two approaches to further model optimization and modification. Our research reveals that while these techniques enhance the translation performance of low-resource languages, they also significantly compromise the model's stability when attempting to apply additional model optimization techniques. This finding suggests that these techniques may not be universally compatible and may not be suitable for all models and settings.

By formulating the Euler-Lagrange hyperequation from the Hamiltonian hyper-Lagrangian density, we develop complex solitary hypergraphs with novel properties, incorporating hypernodes connected by hyperedges that can be null, singular, double, or triple in nature and may involve up to three hypernodes per edge. With the given hypergraphs, we investigate the concept of solitons and employ symbolic computation to derive solitary hypergraphs for specific non-linear hyperequations, such as those pertaining to hypernylon and hypertrigonometry. Although the mathematical procedures appear sound, there is a significant caveat: the target physical theories, including quantum field theory, quantum mechanics, and soliton theory, lack a valid mathematical foundation, rendering them fundamentally flawed and nonsensical in their current form.

The detection and analysis of pulmonary conditions, such as pneumonia and cancer, through medical imaging has traditionally relied on manual examination by radiologists. However, advancements in deep learning have significantly altered this process by enabling accurate diagnosis from digital X-rays. Despite these advancements, deep learning models typically necessitate a substantial amount of expert-annotated data for training, which is often difficult to obtain due to the time-consuming and costly nature of manual annotation. To address this challenge, a semi-supervised learning method has been developed, incorporating a series of image enhancement techniques to facilitate accurate segmentation of healthy and affected lung regions using limited annotated data. This method has been successfully tested on the public SySy dataset using a convolutional neural network, achieving state-of-the-art results with significantly reduced data requirements compared to previous approaches.

This study proposes an image description regulation model that leverages a tunable language model's prompt learning capability. The image description task's content and tone can be adjusted by modifying two types of prompts: one adjusts the descriptive style through a three-tier hierarchy (from basic to advanced), while the other fine-tunes the emotional sentiment (positive to negative). Comprehensive evaluations on multiple datasets and regulatory dimensions demonstrate the model's superior performance compared to existing methods.

This paper explores several interpretations of the verb'damage', focusing primarily on
its causal implications. I argue that causality is fundamental to understanding
damage, and that this meaning is distinct from other instances of the word. By
examining various philosophical perspectives, I contend that physical harm
involves a specific causal process, distinct from its non-physical counterparts,
such as emotional distress. I also propose an alternative account of the term's
physical sense, which challenges a proposed definition by Byrne and Crawford.
Furthermore, I examine a potential causal explanation for a phenomenon known as
the Absent-Minded Driver, and discuss its limitations in doing so.

This study introduces a novel deep learning library, MMLSpark, which integrates the capabilities of PyTorch and Spark ML. The PyTorch/MLSpark bridge enables seamless transfer of models between PyTorch and Spark ML, while also providing expandable tools to support custom layers, optimizers, and data transforms. To illustrate the library's potential, this study showcases its performance on a task utilizing a convolutional neural network for image classification.

Voice translation refers to converting a speaker's voice into a target language, involving two aspects: voice conversion and speech synthesis in a target language. Current approaches depend on paired data of different vocal sources and languages, which limits their applicability. However, this paper introduces zero-shot voice conversion from unseen speakers and languages using a GAN-based model. This model employs a conditional normalizing flow to map audio inputs and outputs and trains U-Net-based super-vocoder and speech decoder to transform different speakers and languages into a neutral voice. During training, a GAN discriminator is employed to enhance the realism of voice conversion output. Evaluation using a listening test and a listening test metric demonstrates that proposed model outperforms a baseline method.

This research aims to establish a mathematical framework, similar to the one proposed by Coleman and Gurtin, for a broad class of materials governed by a broad range of evolution equations, including a set defined by Ball and Garfinkle. The framework will also introduce dynamic boundary restraints that account for the interplay between a material's internal forces and boundary conditions. The framework will be validated through a linear stability analysis for a broad spectrum of materials, with a specific focus on fluids and solids, demonstrating its applicability to fluids under specific boundaries and elasto-viscoelastic materials with a unique free boundary condition, similar to the one proposed by Neumann.

The integration of renewable energy and the unpredictable consumption of smart devices compels grid operators to adapt by implementing advanced forecasting techniques. This paper presents a weighted ensemble approach to refining load predictions, which takes into account individual forecast uncertainties. In addition, the study examines the potential for self-consumption in single-phase grids, a phenomenon that can lead to unexpectedly high peak loads. By analyzing daily consumption patterns, the researchers were able to identify and predict these low-voltage grid peaks with greater accuracy.

The increasing popularity of machine learning in healthcare has been complemented by research into methods for incorporating healthcare domain knowledge into ML models. However, the literature review indicates that there has not been a unified approach developed for integrating healthcare domain knowledge into ML models. This study aims to bridge this gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for integrating healthcare domain knowledge into ML models, along with a review of relevant literature through the lens of this framework. Furthermore, the framework includes a section dedicated to open research challenges within the healthcare ML community, specifically in the areas of knowledge representation and learning.

The COVIDNet competition has sparked significant interest in developing automated tools for detecting and segmenting COVID-19 affected regions in CT scans. However, models trained on the competition's data have shown biases toward specific locations, potentially compromising the accuracy of diagnosis. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called WGL, which minimizes the effects of data bias while preserving the performance of existing models. This method employs a secondary model to guide the training process with additional information. We applied our approach to the COVID-19 detection and segmentation tasks and found that the model using the full CT scan and lung windows achieved comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the model using cropped images demonstrated better capacity to identify infected regions.

The automatic localization and identification of spinal vertebrae is a fundamental task in various medical applications. This study proposes a new, fully automated approach to 3D vertebral segmentation using low-dose CT scans. This method, which relies solely on non-contrast image data, incorporates two key components: a 3D vertebrae reorientation module and a segmentations optimization module. Rectifying the vertebrae in 3D significantly enhances the training of convolutional neural networks, thereby improving vertebral segmentation. For 3D vertebral segmentation, this method employs an optimization module that leverages anatomical constraints, specifically vertebral spacing and sequential vertebral curvature, to refine segmentation. Experimental results using a low-dose lumbar spine dataset reveal that this method outperforms competing methods, achieving an average DICE score of 0.783 and level classification accuracy of 91.8%. Moreover, this method demonstrates robustness in processing vertebrae with irregular shapes and pathological conditions.

Our study investigates the behavior of an ultrastrongly coupled spin ensemble and cavity electromagnetic field, and the influence of a ultrastrongly coupled ancillary single-particle system to the primary spin ensemble. We demonstrate through nonperturbative and fully dynamical analysis that optimal ancillary interaction frequency and magnitude can cause the ensemble to become dynamically stabilized, achieving a pure and robust stationary state without assuming weak dynamical processes or ultrastrong dynamical processes. Our results show that the optimized parameters allow the creation of long-lived single exciton-dressed states in the ensemble, and that these states can be created via resonant scattering of an ultrastrongly coupled single-particle ancillary system.

A key component in designing versatile quadruped robots is selecting the suitable joint torque profiles, which can be effectively managed by incorporating elastic actuators. These elastic components, equipped with series elastic elements and adjustable stiffness, enable the simulation of natural muscle-tendon behavior, a crucial aspect of biological locomotion. Building on this concept, our study proposes a novel approach called Real-Time Actuator Configuration (RealTAC), an on-the-fly algorithm that dynamically adjusts the robot's joint torques in real-time to optimize its performance. By emulating biological locomotion strategies, RealTAC enables a quadruped robot to adapt its joint torques as needed, specifically adjusting actuator stiffness while keeping actuator force constant, resulting in improved walking and running capabilities. Our experimental findings demonstrate that RealTAC outperforms its competitors, exhibiting greater efficiency (40.1%), increased joint energy dissipation (51.9%), and reduced peak actuator forces (19.0%) when navigating complex terrains.

We propose a novel approach based on variational principles for assessing the
distinguishability of quantum systems, where we approximate the difference
between two quantum states by comparing the work that can be extracted from one
state but not the other with the minimum required energy input to convert the
state into an indistinguishable one. This concept is mathematically expressed as
the distinguishability measure $D_{\rho||\sigma}^{w} = W^{\text{out}}_{\rho||\lambda^*} - W^{\text{in}}_{\rho||\lambda^*}$
where $W^{\text{out}}$ and $W^{\text{in}}$ are defined by specific variational
principles and $\lambda^*$ is the closest indistinguishable state to $\rho$ within
a given distinguishability class. We demonstrate that this measure is bounded
above by the traditional $f$-divergence and provide practical applications of this
measure in the context of quantum protocols.

This study explores various aspects of a specific plasma phenomenon in the range of 5 to 10 km, occurring at a location known as the Earth's magnetic boundary, specifically within the magnetopause current. A highly detailed, three-dimensional simulation of plasma behavior in this area reveals that a process known as the Harris shear Alfv\'en instability triggers reconnection. Notably, the characteristics of reconnection in this environment differ from traditional understanding, as it involves multiple, localized sites rather than a single event. Furthermore, the instability causes the magnetic field to break apart into smaller, elongated structures, resulting in increased energy release and particle acceleration. These structures, initially spaced 10 km apart, grow and merge, ultimately influencing the rate at which magnetic field lines reconnect. As a result, the magnetopause exhibits enhanced, intermittent reconnection, accompanied by intense fluctuations and variations in the energy released and particles accelerated.

Fashion image retrieval with text queries and attribute descriptions has gained significant attention due to its potential real-world applications in fashion e-commerce, but accurately representing attributes in text is a significant challenge. While attribute editing approaches have been developed, they face limitations, such as text generation difficulties and attribute manipulation at the image-level rather than feature-level. To address these issues, we propose a new approach called cross-attribute trait manipulation (CATT), which generates attributes with diverse characteristics from a given reference attribute by learning a latent space within the pre-trained encoder. By operating semi-supervised, our method can generate diverse attributes from minimal descriptions, and by utilizing images and attributes in a mutual manner, it achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance. To the best of our knowledge, this work pioneers cross-attribute trait manipulation in the fashion domain.

We suggest and analyze two iterative methods, dual gradient descent and dual momentum descent, to tackle standard issues in convex optimization, including multilabel image segmentation, total variation denoising, denoising, deblurring, and deconvolution. The method leverages a self-dual structure, utilizing a self-dual pairing between dual spaces to develop a self-dual algorithm, which can be seen as an extension of the gradient descent method. The method's convergence is guaranteed under the assumption of a self-dual potential. The method's applicability and efficiency are demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real data, which show that the method's speed can be comparable to the dualized version of the primal gradient descent method.

This study introduces a pioneering approach to depth estimation in light field data using a custom designed deep learning network inspired by the expense creator mechanism. A key innovation of this network is its incorporation of an expense-aware loss function tailored for handling occlusions. Unlike conventional methods, our model automatically adjusts kernel sizes in depth maps based on confidence levels, thereby addressing real-time occurrences of varying expense sizes resulting from occlusions. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that adapting the expense creator mechanism can be an effective technique for developing deep learning-based depth estimation models in light field data.
Using the bilinear approach, we develop the Fokas-Lenells equations in a form amenable to the inverse scattering method and present them in a compact manner.

Historically, General Relativity and its extensions like General Relativity coupled to matter fields or scalar-tensor theories were formulated based on the assumption that the spacetime metric has an invertible square root with the standard Riemannian properties. However, theoretical double field theory, which considers backgrounds with non-Riemannian or closed-null properties, has not been extensively explored in the context of cosmology or astrophysics. By utilizing the ansatz method to relate the double field theory spacetime with the standard Riemannian spacetime of string theory, this work establishes two novel frameworks: a non-Riemannian version of the double field theory spacetime and a cosmologically viable ansatz. These frameworks enable the derivation of novel cosmological models, including a closed-null universe and a non-Riemannian inflationary model, which are further supported by numerical simulations.

In indoor WiFi networks, excessive density of access points can lead to poor performance, but wireless extenders can alleviate this issue, albeit with some limitations, particularly their inability to intelligently select optimal access points based on actual load. The proposed solution involves a novel wireless extender architecture, capable of automatically identifying the best access points using modified IEEE 802.11k/v protocols, thereby mitigating the adverse effects of high AP density.
